docs.title: Home
docs.text: Stenopos is a platform built so that an attack has nowhere to get through. It is three things that are designed together:

docs.title: Stenopos
docs.text: Ἀσφάλεια περὶ πλείστου · Security above all

docs.title: Stenopos OS
docs.text: A memory-safe, capability-based operating system: a small verified nucleus, every driver and service in its own compartment, and no root. It runs native apps, Debian packages and Windows programs.

docs.title: The Stenopos language
docs.text: The systems language the whole platform is written in. Memory safety, taint tracking, effect and capability types and constant-time secrets are checked by the compiler. Released today through Syntagma.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text: A shell, terminal, editor, browser, mail, calendar, app store and media player. Every one is an ordinary sandboxed package that you can remove or replace.

docs.title: What you can use today
docs.text:
The language and its toolchain are in release candidates:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh
tagma new hello && cd hello && tagma run

See Install, or the latest release. The OS and the apps are designed and not yet built; their pages explain the design. Status shows where every part stands.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Please do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues.

Report them privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting: open the affected repository on GitHub, go to Security, and choose Report a vulnerability. Include steps to reproduce, the affected versions and, if you can, a proof of concept.

We will acknowledge your report, keep you informed, and credit you when the fix is released, unless you prefer to remain anonymous.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
Stenopos OS comes with a suite of first-party apps. None of them is special: each is an ordinary, sandboxed .pano package that declares its capabilities like any other app, and each can be removed or replaced.

App What it is Hoplite (hop) The command shell Kopis The terminal Laconic The text and code editor Periplus The web browser and its memory-safe engine Keryx Mail and messaging Hemera The calendar Agora The app store Lyra The media player

Everyday utilities use plain names, so nobody has to learn a word to find them: Files, Settings, Updates, Passwords, Backup and Terminal.

docs.title: Planned
docs.text:
Everything a desktop is expected to have is planned as part of the system, written for it in Stenopos:

  • To be usable at all: setup and recovery, a viewer for PDF and office documents and images, screenshots, archives, a calculator, a clock, contacts, notes, tasks, a system monitor that shows what each app can touch, disks, printers and scanners, a camera, offline help, a screen reader, magnifier and on-screen keyboard, and fonts.

  • Soon after: an office suite (documents, spreadsheets, presentations, using OpenDocument and reading and writing Word, Excel and PowerPoint files), photos, music and recording, maps and weather, remote desktop, virtual machines, calls, a firewall and VPN, an authenticator, books, and developer tools.

  • Typesetting: engines of our own that run LaTeX documents (with the existing LaTeX packages unchanged) and Typst documents, and a collaborative editor for them that also works offline.

Software that already exists elsewhere is rewritten in Stenopos, not carried over as C or C++: redesigned so each part holds only the permissions it needs, with the bugs found on the way fixed, and tested against the original until the results agree. Where a part is rewritten from another project's source it keeps that project's licence (a driver rewritten from Linux stays GPL), so the system as a whole is under several open-source licences, each part stating its own.

Until one of ours is ready, you can install the original as an ordinary, confined app: LibreOffice, Chromium, Firefox, and Signal Desktop. Signal's protocol is public, and a native Signal client is planned inside Keryx.

docs.title: Publishing your own
docs.text: Anyone can publish a program for Stenopos OS, with no permission from anyone: from your own site or repository, signed with your own key, or through Agora for a listing. Either way, the person installing it sees exactly what it asks to touch first, and it gets nothing else.

docs.title: What every app gets
docs.text:
• Only what it declares. An app's manifest lists its capabilities, and you approve them, often at first use. Files come through the system file chooser, one at a time.
  • No silent network access, no reading other apps' windows, keystrokes or clipboard, and an unspoofable indicator whenever the camera, microphone or screen is in use.
  • Any language. Apps can be written in Stenopos or in C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift, Python, JavaScript or C#, with the same sandbox for all.

docs.title: Hoplite
docs.text:
Designed

Hoplite (hop) is the native command shell. It is structured: commands pass typed records and tables to each other, not text.

ls | where size > 10MB | sort-by modified

Output is a table for people, and to json, to csv or to text for programs.

docs.title: Capability-aware
docs.text:
Each command runs with only the capabilities its command line grants, plus those its manifest declares and you have approved. For example, compress ./photos -o out.zip can read ./photos and write out.zip, and nothing else.

  • Scripts declare what they need in a header. Running a downloaded script shows exactly what it will be able to touch, before it runs, and it cannot exceed that.
  • Arguments are passed as typed values and never re-split or re-parsed, so argument injection is impossible by construction.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text: The scripting language is typed, with Stenopos-like syntax and safe quoting by construction. A script can grow into a compiled Stenopos program with few changes.

docs.title: Working with Linux tools
docs.text: bash, zsh, fish and the GNU tools run in Linux environments. The lx command opens one or runs a Linux command, and pipes cross between Hoplite and Linux commands, converting text to records where the format is known (JSON, CSV and common tools).

docs.title: System commands
docs.text: sten info (security tier and attestation), sten caps (grants), sten logs, sten update and sten env (Linux and Windows environments) all give structured output.

docs.text:
Not started

Not started

docs.title: What it will get from the platform
docs.text:
• Attachments are scanned on arrival by Phalanx Scan, in a sandbox with no capabilities.
  • Messages are parsed by memory-safe parsers, and everything from the network is tainted.
  • Passwords and tokens live in the system secrets store, and network access is limited to the mail servers you configure.

docs.title: Kopis
docs.text:
Designed

Kopis is the terminal: native, GPU-rendered through Eikon, and fast enough to meet the platform's latency and memory budgets.

docs.title: Escape sequences are hostile input
docs.text:
Terminals have a long history of escape-sequence injection bugs, where printing a malicious file makes the terminal act. Kopis parses every escape sequence as tainted input:

  • dangerous sequences, such as writing to the clipboard (OSC 52), title and report queries that echo input back, and hyperlinks, are filtered or need a capability;
  • inline images (sixel and kitty-style) are decoded in a sandbox.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Full Unicode, ligatures and true colour, with Hoplite as the default shell and Linux shells available in Linux environments.

docs.text:

  • The Stenopos language server (stenopos lsp) for diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition and completion.
  • Text rendering and input through Morphe, with full Unicode, right-to-left scripts and sandboxed input methods.

docs.title: Lyra
docs.text:
Designed

Lyra is the media player, and the media framework every app uses to play and record audio and video.

docs.title: Built to open hostile files safely
docs.text:
• Files and streams are parsed by memory-safe Stenopos parsers in short-lived sandboxes with no capabilities, so a malicious video has nothing to attack and nothing to reach.
  • Hardware decoding is isolated, and decoded frames travel to the screen without copies.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
Files Format .mp4, .m4v, .m4a, .mov MP4 and QuickTime .mkv, .webm Matroska and WebM .ogg, .opus, .oga Ogg .ts, .m2ts MPEG transport stream .mp3, .flac, .aac, .wav, .aiff Audio files

Formats are recognised by their content, not their file name, and an unrecognised file is refused rather than guessed at.

docs.title: Codecs
docs.text:
Nothing in the base OS needs a patent licence:

Codec How it's decoded AV1, VP8, VP9, Opus, Vorbis, FLAC, MP3 Built in H.264, HEVC The device's hardware decoder where it has one; otherwise an opt-in codec package AAC The opt-in codec package, until its remaining patents lapse

The codec package is an ordinary signed package, offered the first time you open a file that needs it and installed only if you agree. Its decoders run in the same sandboxes. DRM is optional and confined.

docs.title: How it fits
docs.text: Lyra decodes. Aulos plays the sound on the right output, and Skene and Eikon show the video.

docs.title: Periplus
docs.text:
Designed

Periplus is the web engine of Stenopos OS: new, memory-safe, written in Stenopos, and the only engine in the system. Like the rest of the OS, it is ours.

Chromium and Firefox are not part of the system. You can install either as an app, confined like any other software you add, and both also run unmodified in a Linux environment.

docs.title: Double sandboxing
docs.text: On Stenopos OS every site's renderer holds an empty capability set: no file, network, device or IPC access except channels to the browser's own processes. That is on top of the browser's own sandbox, so escaping it gains nothing.

docs.title: The Periplus engine
docs.text:
Periplus is compartmentalized per site. Every byte from the network is tainted, cookies and credentials are secret[T], and rendering, networking and TLS go through the OS's own Eikon, Dromos and Skytale.

It is delivered component by component, and each one hardens the whole OS as soon as it is ready:

Component Used across the OS for Image decoders (PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, SVG) All image decoding and thumbnails Font parsing and text shaping The UI toolkit and the terminal Media parsers The media framework HTML, CSS, URL and JSON parsers Help, rich text and manifests A JavaScript engine App scripting Layout and rendering Rich documents and the help viewer

Periplus is the system's browser and its web view's engine from the first release that has one. What it can render grows release by release, measured by Web Platform Tests and a corpus of top sites.

docs.title: Periplus WebView
docs.text: Apps that show web content use the system web view, a shared runtime patched once for every app. It is Periplus. An app that needs something Periplus can't render yet says so; the system never falls back to a foreign engine behind your back.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
Stenopos OS is one operating system built into profiles for different devices. Each profile is the same verified system with a different set of parts compiled in. There is never a "lite" version with weaker security.

Profile For Idle memory target Desktops and laptops x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V machines ≤ 400 MiB (1 GiB minimum RAM) Servers Cloud, bare metal, Kubernetes nodes ≤ 128 MiB Raspberry Pi Pi 3, 4 and 5, Zero 2 W ≤ 300 MiB as a desktop Embedded: Lochos Industrial, IoT, kiosks ≤ 32 MiB, in a ≤ 16 MiB image Phones and tablets: Trireme Phones with owner-enrolled boot keys (Phase 7)

docs.title: Security tiers
docs.text:
What the hardware can do decides how strong the isolation is, and Stenopos OS tells you which tier a machine runs at (on the boot screen, in Settings and with sten info):

Tier Needs Means 1: Full Compartment isolation, an IOMMU for every DMA-capable device, control-flow integrity in hardware, and a TPM Every guarantee in force 2: Strong Isolation and an IOMMU, but no hardware CFI or no TPM DMA isolation in force; less exploit hardening or no attestation 3: Mediated Isolation without an IOMMU (for example a Raspberry Pi 4) A verified DMA mediator checks device access; any driver it can't mediate is named as trusted

The tier is derived from the hardware at boot, never assumed, and recorded in the measured boot state so that a remote party can verify it. Policy can require a minimum tier: a password vault, for example, can insist on Tier 2.

All profiles are 64-bit and need an MMU with no-execute pages.

docs.title: Desktops and laptops
docs.text:
The full Stenopos Desktop on x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V machines.

Budget Target Idle memory ≤ 400 MiB Minimum RAM 1 GiB (never more than 2 GiB) Boot to login, after firmware (NVMe) ≤ 3 s

Laptops get per-app energy accounting, power management for the CPU and devices, and battery, thermal and fan control through Krepis. Firmware updates for UEFI, SSDs, docks and peripherals are part of the system's own updates.

A PC with an IOMMU, a TPM and hardware control-flow integrity runs at Tier 1.

The desktop arrives in Phase 5 of the roadmap.

docs.title: Stenopos Lochos
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos Lochos is the embedded and industrial profile: the same verified OS, compiled down to a minimal image. It is named for the smallest Spartan unit.

Budget Target Image size ≤ 16 MiB RAM, minimal headless device ≤ 32 MiB Interrupt-to-task latency (Pi-class hardware) ≤ 10 µs

docs.title: Hardware, one capability at a time
docs.text: GPIO, I²C, SPI, UART, PWM, ADC and DAC, CAN, 1-Wire and industrial Ethernet are capabilities per pin, channel, bus or device. An app controlling a motor gets that PWM channel and its GPIO pins, and nothing else.

docs.title: Built to run unattended
docs.text:
• Hard real time with guaranteed scheduling budgets, isolated from networking, logging and updates.
  • A hardware watchdog supervised by the nucleus, restartable compartments, and automatic rollback of failed updates.
  • A flash-wear-aware mode and safety on power loss.
  • Fleet updates: signed delta updates with staged rollout, resumable over poor links.
  • A signed lockdown policy: no shell, no SSH, a fixed set of apps, an allowlist of ports, debug interfaces off.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Every device has its own identity key, bound to hardware where possible, for attestation-based enrollment. There are no shared default passwords, ever.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
MQTT over TLS 1.3, OPC UA, Modbus, CANopen and Matter/Thread, each a sandboxed component with scoped network and bus capabilities.

Microcontrollers without an MMU can't provide the isolation model, so they are out of scope; they talk to Lochos devices over these protocols.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Stenopos OS supports the Raspberry Pi 3, 4 and 5 and the Zero 2 W, as a desktop, a server or an embedded device. Older 32-bit models (the Pi 1 and the original Zero) are not supported.

Budget Target Idle memory as a desktop ≤ 300 MiB Minimum RAM as a desktop 1 GiB Boot to login, after firmware (Pi 5) ≤ 6 s

docs.title: Security on a Pi
docs.text:
The Pi 4 has no IOMMU, so it runs at Tier 3: a verified DMA mediator checks every device access it can, and the tier report names any driver it can't. The Pi 5's IOMMU support is limited. Stenopos OS shows you exactly which tier your board runs at.

Pi firmware (the EEPROM) is updated through Krepis, like any other firmware. HAT overlays are applied declaratively and validated.

The Raspberry Pi 5 is one of the first two real-hardware targets, in Phase 3 of the roadmap.

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
The server profile is headless and minimal, and it is the first public release of Stenopos OS (Phase 4 of the roadmap).

Budget Target Idle memory (SSH, network and storage) ≤ 128 MiB Minimum RAM 256 MiB Boot to ready, after firmware ≤ 2 s

docs.title: Managing a server
docs.text:
• Over SSH, which stays off until you configure it, with Hoplite and the sten commands.
  • Declarative configuration. The whole server state (packages, services, network, capability grants and policies) is one signed config file. It is applied atomically, reproducible across a fleet, and rolled back through snapshots.
  • Remote attestation. Clusters and orchestrators can refuse any node that isn't running a verified image at the required security tier.
  • The LTS channel gives five years or more of updates.

docs.title: Workloads
docs.text: Unmodified Docker and OCI images run in Oikos without a Linux kernel, Debian environments run apt-get as usual, and a Kubernetes-compatible node agent joins existing clusters. Stenopos OS also runs well as a guest on KVM, Hyper-V, VMware and Xen.

docs.title: Stenopos Trireme
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos Trireme is the profile for phones and tablets, named for the fast Greek warship. It is designed now and built in Phase 7 of the roadmap.

docs.title: The modem is hostile
docs.text: The cellular modem is treated as a hostile network device: confined by the IOMMU to its own buffers, driven by its own compartment, and everything it sends is tainted. The OS keeps control of the modem's power, so airplane mode can cut it off entirely where the hardware allows.

docs.title: Phone features
docs.text:
• Calls (VoLTE, VoNR), SMS and MMS, RCS where possible, eSIM and dual SIM.
  • Emergency calls always work, even when locked and without a SIM.
  • The call log, messages and contacts are capabilities, granted per app.
  • One end-to-end encrypted push channel, compatible with UnifiedPush and self-hostable, so apps don't poll and nothing depends on Google or Apple.
  • Location, NFC and background sensor access are capabilities, with an indicator for location that apps cannot hide.
  • A phone shell built on the Tablet layout. Docking to a display switches to the desktop.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text: Trireme targets phones that let the owner enroll their own verified-boot keys: Google Pixel devices, Fairphone, and Linux phones such as the PinePhone and Librem 5.

docs.title: Language & Toolchain
docs.text:
Stenopos language: In progress Syntagma: In progress

Stenopos is the systems language the whole platform is written in. Its files are .sten. It reads like C, with braces, C-style declarations and no semicolons, and it makes security part of the type system:

  • Memory safety without a garbage collector. NOVA ownership tracking frees memory at compile-time-known points and rules out use-after-free and double frees for everything the test corpus covers. Using a value after send moved it is a compile error (from rc.8). Threads share state only through chan, atomic and the locks; a data-race-freedom guarantee is planned, not yet checked.
  • Taint tracking. For functions you mark @tainted (sources) and @sink, the compiler refuses a path from one to the other that doesn't pass a @sanitizer. The standard library's own sources and sinks (arguments, environment, stdin, files, sockets, the shell) are not marked yet; they will be by 1.0.
  • Effects and capabilities. A function declares what it may do (@cap(File), @cap(Network)…), and the compiler holds it to that.
  • Constant-time secrets. secret[T] values cannot steer branches or memory access, so they cannot leak through timing.
  • Contracts, null safety and checked integer overflow, by default.
func main() -> int32 {
    str name = "Sparta"
    println("Hello, {name}!")
    return 0
}

docs.title: The toolchain: Syntagma
docs.text:
The language ships through Syntagma: the compiler (stenopos), the build tool (tagma), the standard library and the language server, released together under one version. See Syntagma, tagma and stenopos.

The compiler is self-hosting: it is written in Stenopos and compiles itself, and it builds for six Linux architectures.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Found by the review of 2026-11-14 (design/REVIEW-2026-11-14.md). The first two are in rc.6: don't run rc.6's tagma check, tagma build or stenopos check on a project tree you don't trust.

  • Commands from names in a project tree (RV-C1, in rc.6): tagma check/build and stenopos check built shell command lines from paths and names, so $(...) in a path dependency, the package name or a directory name ran. Every value is now quoted as one shell word (one helper, sh_quote), the package name is checked on every command (letters, digits, -, _), and the bootstrap builds a hostile tree and fails if anything runs. (rc.8 drops the shell from the toolchain altogether.)
  • Use-after-free through !! (RV-C2, in rc.6): Node x = n!! on a nullable struct handed out the nullable's own box, so reassigning n freed what x pointed to, and two n!! bindings were one value. !! now gives a copy (or takes over an owned temporary), as ?? and narrowing do (example nonnull_assert_copies).
  • A server killed by its own error handling (RV-C3): an uncaught throw in any task called abort(), and accept threw when the process ran out of descriptors, so a few hundred idle connections stopped any std.http service. An uncaught throw now ends the program cleanly (exit 70, the message, output flushed, workers retired, no core dump; documented), and accept waits through descriptor or memory exhaustion (warning at most every 10 s) and skips clients that gave up.
  • Request and response splitting (RV-C4): std.http sent CR and LF from the program as they were. fetch now refuses a method that isn't a token, a URL with a space or control character, and a header with a CR, LF or NUL; respond sends a 500 instead of a header like that (and says why on stderr), so a value taken from the request can't add headers.
  • Headers read differently from other parsers (found by httpfuzz): std.http trimmed control bytes away, so it read Content-Length: 1 followed by a control byte as 1, and a chunk-size line 0, CR, control byte as 0, where Python's http.client refuses both. A parser that accepts what a stricter one refuses is a smuggling risk. Requests and responses with any control byte but tab in the start line or headers are now refused, and chunk-size lines are parsed strictly (hex digits, then only spaces or tabs before a ; extension).
  • TLS setup fails closed, and handles can't be reused (RV-H4): a failed SSL_set1_host, minimum-version, SSL_set_fd or SNI step now stops the connection instead of continuing with less checking; std.tls speaks TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only (ADR-0046); and each handle carries a generation, so closing or using a stale TlsConn fails instead of reaching the connection that reused its slot.
  • Unchecked allocations (RV-H6): the runtime checked 3 of its 85 allocations. Every one now goes through kxmalloc/kxcalloc/ kxrealloc/kxstrdup, which stop the program with stenopos: out of memory; scripts/ci-runtime-lint.sh (CI) fails on a bare allocation. The scheduler's setup (epoll, eventfd, worker threads) stops with the reason when it fails instead of leaving tasks that never run.
  • exit() gives busy workers 1 s; it no longer runs OpenSSL's cleanup when one of them didn't stop and could still be inside TLS (RV-M5). tagma's log tee waits at most 1 s for its thread at exit, so a daemon started by a build step that keeps stderr open can't hang tagma (RV-M4).

Costs and follow-ups of these fixes: the clean exit on an uncaught throw adds 183 bytes of code; the map benchmark sat 71 bytes under a page boundary, so its release binary is one page (4 KB) larger and the baseline is re-recorded (the other workloads are unchanged, because each subsystem now registers its exit work when first used instead of being named by the exit path). The audit probe mem-spawn-moves moved from MISCOMPILE to ACCEPTED when spawn learned str arguments: still ADR-0040's missing use-after-move check. A function execute_with uses was called without a declaration (an error for newer C compilers): declared.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• std.http reads framing strictly (RFC 9112), refusing what two parsers could read differently (the way requests are smuggled): a bare CR or LF or a NUL in the headers, folded header lines, header names that aren't tokens, a malformed or conflicting Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding with Content-Length, a transfer coding other than chunked (501), request lines and status lines that aren't HTTP/1.0 or 1.1, a status that isn't three digits, chunk data longer than its size. A 1xx, 204 or 304 response has no body whatever its headers say. Found by httpfuzz.
  • Memory left at exit: exit() now retires the worker threads first (their resolver, OpenSSL and loader state were left behind), stops the signal forwarder, and frees the main thread's try/catch buffers, as a normal return now does too. Every new program is clean under valgrind with all leak kinds shown.
  • A program's own functions were taken as part of the last module it imported, so one named like a function of that module (rfc3339 beside import std.time) was "duplicate function 'rfc3339' in module 'std.time'" (example names_like_std).
  • Imported modules were ordered breadth-first: when the program imported both std.http and std.net, std.http came before std.net, so its use of Conn was "unknown type". Files are now placed after everything they import.
  • read_file read files by their reported size, so /proc and /sys files (size 0) read as "" (example read_proc_file).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Programs start once, on the system's stack. Every program raised its stack limit to 1 GiB and executed itself again before main, so a hello-world took 1.7 times as long as C's (3.1 ms against 1.8 ms; the benchmark ran under valgrind, where that step is skipped, and never saw it). A program now gets the system's stack (usually 8 MiB) unless it asks for more: [build] stack = "256MiB" in Tagma.toml, or --stack <size> on stenopos build and --multi. The compiler and tagma ask for 1 GiB. Running out of stack on the main thread says stack overflow and how to get more, after flushing output, instead of a bare segmentation fault. Programs the toolchain starts (tagma run, tagma test, stenopos run) get the stack limit the toolchain started with, not its 1 GiB.
  • Allocation: stenopos_alloc is malloc, one test and a return (the zero-size and out-of-memory cases on a cold path); the runtime calls libc through the GOT (-fno-plt), not PLT stubs; integers become strings without a copy; map keys are copied inline again. With every allocation checked (RV-H6), the benchmarks run fewer instructions than before (map -2.3%, strings -2.8%, structs -0.9%), no binary grew, and the IR the compiler emits is unchanged. (A NULL test inlined into the program's IR was tried first: it ran faster but cost opt and llc 12% more work on struct-heavy programs.)
  • tests/bench/run.sh --record keeps, for each number, the lower of the baseline and the new measurement: the baseline is a ceiling, tightened by improvements and never loosened by a regression.
  • The compiler and tagma linked OpenSSL: the driver's search for a TLS call found its own search text, a string constant in them. Found by the benchmark gate (3M more instructions per build); the bootstrap now checks which binaries link OpenSSL.
  • Breaking: the HTTP client moved to std.http.client (ClientRequest, request, get, post, post_json, fetch); std.http keeps the messages, the server, parse_url and parse_response. A server that never makes requests no longer links OpenSSL.
  • OpenSSL is linked, not loaded with dlopen (ADR-0046): the compiler adds libssl.so.3 and libcrypto.so.3 to programs that use TLS, and no program links libdl. A missing libssl is now reported by the loader at start, not on the first connection, and a program that uses TLS leaves nothing behind at exit under valgrind.
  • Standard output is flushed line by line when it goes to a pipe or a socket (ADR-0044 D12), so a service's output reaches kubectl logs, journald or | grep as each line is printed. A terminal was already line-buffered; a file or /dev/null stays fully buffered.
  • str.index_of skips to candidates with memchr instead of comparing at every position (the compiler searches its whole output once per build).
  • Breaking: std.http is now a server and client (below). Its old response(status, body) -> str is response(status, content_type, body) -> Response, and text(status, body) replaces it for plain text; parse_request(raw) stays, returning the fuller Request.
  • tagma's status lines (Compiling, Finished, Running, Added, Updated, Fetched...) go to stderr, so tagma run > out.txt holds only the program's output. tagma resolve's answer stays on stdout. Found by the new end-to-end test.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• tagma doc --prepare and --check. Prepare gives every file, type, function and method a /// doc block: a plain // comment block directly above an item (or a file's header above module) becomes its doc, and an item with none gets a /// TODO: stub. Check fails while a public item (or the file) has no doc or only a stub. std went through it: every public item in std is documented, 1,100 lines of comments became docs.
  • The doc generator: a /// block above annotations (@cap(File)) is the function's (annotations used to cut it off, so every function with a capability lost its docs); a /// block above module describes the module; a blank line ends a doc block; doc lines keep their indentation and line breaks (Markdown paragraphs, lists and code).
  • std.http accepts chunked request bodies (decoded as they arrive, within the body limit; trailers read and dropped).
  • scripts/httpfuzz.py (CI's fuzz step): std.http against Python's http.client and http.server, and a live std.http server under mutated and junk requests, sent whole or in pieces.
  • spawn takes str arguments: the task gets its own copy (a temporary moves in, a variable is copied), freed when it returns (example spawn_str_args).
  • Functions can return a channel (or lock, or atomic) they created, and the caller owns it: func start() -> chan[int32] can spawn a worker and hand back its channel; the worker keeps running. chan[int32] c = start() declares one. Returning a channel a function didn't create is refused (example chan_return).
  • std.os.exit_grace(ms): how long a program may wait for its tasks after main returns; past it, the program says so and exits with 124, cleaning up as exit() does. Unset, main's return waits as long as the tasks take. Either way, after 3 s it says what it is waiting for and how to stop.
  • tagma's [output] in Tagma.toml: status = "stderr" | "stdout" | "none" for its progress lines, and log = "<file>" to append each run (the command line, then everything on stderr: tagma's messages, the compiler's diagnostics, a failing llc or cc). --status, -q/--quiet and --log override it for one run. Errors always reach stderr.
  • std.fs.append(path, text): one O_APPEND write. std.io.append_file and std.logging's file logger use it: they used to read and rewrite the whole file for every line (slow as a log grows, and two tasks logging at once could lose lines).
  • std.tls: TLS client connections (k8s-todo item 6), using the system's OpenSSL (3.x or 1.1), loaded with dlopen the first time a program connects, so programs that don't use TLS don't depend on it. verified() checks the chain (system CAs or ca_file) and the host name; pinned(sha256) trusts exactly one certificate, checked after the handshake and before any byte is sent; asking to check nothing throws. TLS 1.2+, SNI; the handshake and reads wait on the poller, so a task doing TLS lets the others run. Failures throw with the reason (certificate not trusted: self-signed certificate, the certificate doesn't match the pin (it is sha256 ...)).
  • std.http: an HTTP/1.1 server and client (k8s-todo item 7). Server: serve(conn, limits()) and next() -> Request? / respond(Response), one Hemerodrome per connection, keep-alive and pipelining, limits on headers (431) and bodies (413), a slow-client deadline, 400 for malformed requests. Client: get, post, post_json, fetch with headers, a deadline and TLS options; Content-Length, chunked and read-to-close bodies. A Kubernetes probe and curl -d @body.json work against it (tests/e2e/service).
  • Signals on a channel: std.os.notify_signals([SIGTERM], ch) forwards watched signals into a chan[int32] the program owns (from a runtime thread, so no task waits forever; forwarding stops when the channel is freed). std.os.exit(code) ends the program now, after flushing output, even while tasks are waiting: it retires the worker threads first, so nothing they hold is left behind (example signals_on_a_channel).
  • The soak test (tests/soak/run.sh): an MQTT reader on a real broker, a publisher, a timer and an HTTP health endpoint for 24 hours, checking the work done, flat memory and a clean SIGTERM.
  • End-to-end tests (tests/e2e/): install follows the docs in a clean container, from the signed installer through a project with a path dependency, a registry package and every tagma command; service builds a small service on std.fs, net, os, time and channels with a given tagma.
  • Channels: c.try_recv() takes an element if one is waiting, and c.recv_timeout(ms) waits at most ms milliseconds; both give T?, null when nothing arrived, for every element type. A Hemerodrome waiting with a deadline parks on the channel and its worker's timers at once, so the others on that worker keep running (example channels_that_wait; stress chan_timeout_stress races sends against deadlines, natively and under Helgrind).
  • Hemerodromes that wait no longer hold their worker thread (GREEN-THREADS phase 3, ADR-0043 §3.5). Each worker has an epoll poller and a timer heap; sleep, socket reads, writes, accepts and connects, recv_timeout, poll, wait_signal and execute's pipes park the waiting Hemerodrome there, and the worker runs the others. A server waiting on a socket, a ticker and a client now run together on one worker, where the server's wait used to hold the only worker and deadlock them (example tasks_that_wait); 2000 sleeping Hemerodromes take one sleep's time. STENOPOS_WORKERS=N fixes the worker count.
  • Running programs without a shell (ADR-0043 §3.6; std 76b1bcc): std.os.execute(["tar", "-czf", out, dir]) and execute_with(argv, ExecOptions { env, dir, stdin }) return Output { code, stdout, stderr }. Nothing in an argument is split, expanded or interpreted; stdout and stderr are read together (neither pipe can fill and stall the child); the child's environment is empty unless given (environ() lists ours); it starts with default signal handling. A program that can't start throws; a non-zero exit is its code. exec(str) stays the shell path.
  • Signals: std.os.watch_signals([SIGTERM, SIGINT]) and wait_signal(ms) -> int32?, so a service finishes its work before exiting on SIGTERM.
  • Host built-ins os_exec, os_environ, os_error, sig_watch and sig_wait (@cap(Process)), as table entries.
  • std.fs (ADR-0043 §3.7, PLAN MS1; std 2e87f1f): read (null when the file is missing, "" when it is empty), write_atomic (a temporary file, fsync, rename, fsync the directory: never a half-written file), list_dir (sorted), stat (size, mtime, mode, kind; links not followed), exists, mkdir_all, rename, remove, remove_all, chmod, temp_dir (mode 0700) and set_umask, all @cap(File); failures throw read /x: permission denied.
  • Octal literals: 0o755, 0o600 (file modes).
  • std.convert.parse_int64 and parse_int32: null for anything but an optional sign and digits, or a value out of range. parse_int and str_to_int are deprecated (ADR-0043 §3.8).
  • Host built-ins are declared in one table (host_builtin in the parser: runtime function, parameters, result, capability, effect), read by every check and by code generation: a new one is a table line and its C function. The twelve fs_* built-ins are the first.
  • std.net by name, IPv4 or IPv6, with deadlines (ADR-0043 §3.4, PLAN MS1; std 0f63911): connect resolves names (getaddrinfo, each address in turn), connect_timeout(host, port, ms), listen on IPv6 and IPv4, listen_on(addr, port), recv_timeout(conn, ms) -> str? (null: nothing in time), poll(conns, ms) and resolve(host). New built-ins net_resolve, net_error, net_set_timeout, tcp_wait, tcp_poll and tcp_listen_on, all @cap(Network).
  • std.time (ADR-0043 §3.3, PLAN MS1): unix(), unix_ms(), mono_ns(), sleep_ms(), the calendar in UTC or the local zone (utc, local, from_utc, DateTime), and format, format_utc, format_local, rfc3339, rfc3339_local. Times are int64 seconds, exact far past 2038; the calendar is computed in Stenopos (std 038d2cf). Built on four new built-ins, clock_unix_ns(), clock_mono_ns(), sleep_ns(int64) and local_offset(int64): no capability (reading the clock is not an effect on the world), but not @pure. Built-in arguments may now be int64, and an integer literal widens to it. Example time_calendar. Sleeping inside a task still blocks its worker thread until the I/O poller lands (GREEN-THREADS phase 3).
  • String escapes \xNN (any byte, two hex digits) and \u{H} (any Unicode character, 1-6 hex digits, as UTF-8), in strings and, when the result is one byte, in character literals (L69). Example string_escapes.
  • @cap takes a list: @cap(File, Process) and @cap(File | Process) mean the same as one @cap per line (L67, found porting Tux). An unknown name or a malformed list is an error. Example cap_lists.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• std.net failures throw, naming the operation, its target and the system's reason: connect mosquitto:1883: connection refused, resolve nas.lan: name not found, connect 10.0.0.9:443: timed out after 5000 ms (audit L70). They returned a handle with fd < 0 and no reason, so a check of fd < 0 no longer fires: catch the exception instead. recv still returns "" at the end of a stream.
  • An unknown escape is an error, listing the valid ones. It used to keep the byte after the backslash silently: "\d" was "d", "\b" was "b", and "\u{80}" became u plus an interpolation (L69).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A temporary string passed to split or replace (s.split(str_from_byte(0))) leaked. Example temp_method_args.
  • Testing a call's nullable result for null inline (show(find(k) == null)) produced invalid IR (the bool was taken for the call's owned string) and leaked the string. The result is dropped after the test. Example null_test_of_call.
  • Writing to a connection the peer had closed raised SIGPIPE, which ended the program: a service died the first time a client or broker went away. It is now an error (send: broken pipe). Socket calls interrupted by a signal are retried, and sockets are closed in child processes.
  • A string with no closing quote crashed the compiler ("array index out of bounds", no location): a string may span lines, but the lexer didn't count the lines inside one, so every later line number was wrong and the parser ran off the end. Lines inside strings are counted, and a string still open at the end of the file is reported where it starts (L65).
  • An unclosed ( or [ is reported on the line where it opened. It used to surface lines later as "unexpected token after statement", because everything after it was read as one expression (L65). Lexical errors are syntax errors (E0200).
  • A top-level function named like a built-in (fail, println, exec, list_new, ...) is refused, naming the built-in. Calls to it went to the built-in: fail, println and list_new silently never called the user's function, and the others were checked against the built-in's parameters (L66). Methods may still use these names.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Each program is written twice, in Stenopos and in C, and both must print the same output. Stenopos builds with stenopos build --release, C with cc -O2 -s. Each cell shows the Stenopos number, then Stenopos ÷ C: below 1× means Stenopos uses less. Instruction counts come from valgrind, so they are exact and repeat run to run. Build counts include the whole toolchain (LLVM, the C compiler, the linker).

Program Binary size Run (instructions) Peak memory Build (instructions) fib 14.0 KB · 0.99× 7.4M · 1.21× 1.4 MB · 0.99× 85.8M · 0.29× hello 14.0 KB · 0.99× 128k · 1.08× 1.4 MB · 1.15× 80.7M · 0.71× loop 14.0 KB · 0.99× 30.9M · 0.95× 1.4 MB · 1.04× 94.2M · 0.71× map 18.0 KB · 1.27× 33.9M · 0.85× 2.4 MB · 0.88× 97.3M · 0.47× sort 14.0 KB · 0.99× 25.0M · 1.09× 1.6 MB · 1.19× 94.3M · 0.60× strings 14.0 KB · 0.99× 13.2M · 0.80× 2.1 MB · 1.44× 92.1M · 0.54× structs 14.0 KB · 0.99× 25.4M · 0.97× 2.7 MB · 1.28× 134.0M · 0.79× Geometric mean 1.03× 0.99× 1.12× 0.56×

Every number is within the budgets we hold ourselves to.

Since v1.0.0-rc.6:

Program Measure v1.0.0-rc.6 Now Change fib compile instructions 36.7M 37.1M +1.1% hello compile instructions 31.8M 32.1M +1.1% map binary size 14.0 KB 18.0 KB +28.5% map run instructions 34.6M 33.9M -2.0% strings run instructions 13.5M 13.2M -2.5%

Measured by CI on commit 6ccf5815e2a5 in Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm), LLVM version 18.1.8, cc (Debian 12.2.0-14+deb12u1) 12.2.0. The numbers and their signature are attached to the release as benchmarks.tsv.

docs.title: Which file do I need?
docs.text:
File What it is syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz Everything: tagma, stenopos, the runtime and the standard library. This is what the installer installs tagma-linux-<arch>, stenopos-linux-<arch> The two commands on their own stenopos-std.tar.gz, stenopos_runtime.c The standard library and the runtime on their own stenopos-bootstrap-seed-x86_64 The seed compiler the self-hosted bootstrap starts from install.sh The installer SHA256SUMS, *.asc Checksums and signatures

Earlier releases: all Syntagma releases.

docs.title: As a project
docs.text:
tagma new hello
cd hello
tagma run

tagma new creates:

hello/
├── Tagma.toml
├── .gitignore
└── src/
    └── main.sten

src/main.sten is the program:

func main() -> void {
    println("Hello from hello!")
}

and tagma run builds it to target/draft/hello and runs it.

docs.title: As a single file
docs.text:
The compiler builds one file with no project:

func main() -> int32 {
    println("Hello, world!")
    return 0
}

stenopos run hello.sten

docs.title: What each line means
docs.text:
• func main() -> int32 { is the entry point. It returns the exit code; -> void means "exit with 0".
  • println(...) prints a line. It is built in, so there is nothing to import, and {...} inside a string interpolates a value.
  • return 0: exit code 0 means success.
  • Braces mark blocks; a new line ends a statement.

docs.title: String interpolation
docs.text:
func main() -> int32 {
    str name = "Stenopos"
    println("Hello, {name}!")
    return 0
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Projects with tagma: dependencies, tests and builds.
  • The Language Guide: variables, types and control flow.

docs.title: The installer (recommended)
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

The installer finds your CPU architecture, downloads the newest Syntagma release (pre-releases included), checks its signature against the Stenopos release key built into the installer, checks the SHA-256 checksum, and installs:

What Where tagma, the build tool /usr/local/bin stenopos, the compiler /usr/local/bin The runtime and the standard library /usr/local/lib/stenopos

Both commands find the runtime and library beside themselves, so nothing needs configuring.

Setting Effect STENOPOS_VERSION=v1.0.0-rc.7 Install a specific release STENOPOS_INSTALL=$HOME/.local/bin Install somewhere else (the library goes in the sibling lib/stenopos) STENOPOS_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1 Refuse to install if gpg is missing and the signature can't be checked

Stenopos needs llc (LLVM 14 or newer) and cc (a C compiler) when it compiles:

sudo apt-get install -y llvm clang     # Debian and Ubuntu
brew install llvm                      # macOS

A program that uses TLS (std.tls, or https with std.http.client) is linked with OpenSSL 3 (libssl.so.3 and libcrypto.so.3), so building and running it needs OpenSSL 3 installed (libssl3 on Debian and Ubuntu, there by default). Programs that don't use TLS don't need it.

docs.title: Supported systems
docs.text: Linux on six architectures: x86_64, aarch64, ppc64le, riscv64, armv7 and s390x, including 32-bit (armv7) and big-endian (s390x). Any of them can cross-compile for the others.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
Each release has a bundle per architecture, syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz, containing bin/tagma, bin/stenopos and lib/stenopos/. Unpack it anywhere and put its bin/ on your PATH:

tar -xzf syntagma-1.0.0-rc.7-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
export PATH="$PWD/syntagma-1.0.0-rc.7-linux-x86_64/bin:$PATH"

See Downloads for the files and how to verify them.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
tagma version
stenopos version

docs.title: How the compiler is built
docs.text: The compiler is written in Stenopos and builds itself. Each release also publishes the seed compiler that its bootstrap starts from (stenopos-bootstrap-seed-x86_64), and every build checks that the compiler, rebuilt by itself, produces identical output. The source is on GitHub, under MIT OR Apache-2.0.

docs.title: If / else
docs.text:
Parentheses around the condition are required:

if (x > 0) {
    println("positive")
} else if (x < 0) {
    println("negative")
} else {
    println("zero")
}

docs.title: Ternary
docs.text:
Coming in 1.0

Not implemented yet.

int32 abs_x = if (x >= 0) x else -x

docs.title: For loops
docs.text:
// 0 through 9: `..` stops before its end
for (i in 0..=10) {
    println("{i}")
}

// 0 through 10: `..=` includes its end
for (i in 0..=10) {
    println("{i}")
}

A range is half-open, as Python's range, Rust's .. and Go's for i := 0; i < n are: 0..n runs n times, so 0..xs.len() visits every index of a list. a..=b includes b; a..<b means the same as a..b. The loop variable has the ends' type (int64 for 0..xs.len()).

From rc.8 (ADR-0044 D8); before, a..b included b.

docs.title: While
docs.text:
while (counter < 100) {
    counter = counter + 1
}

docs.title: Do-while
docs.text:
do {
    counter = counter + 1
} while (counter < 100)

docs.title: Repeat
docs.text:
Coming in 1.0

Not implemented yet.

repeat (5) {
    println("hello")
}

docs.title: Match
docs.text:
A case uses the colon form: the statements after the : run until the next case or the closing }. Patterns are literals, enum variants, or _ for the catch-all.

match (status) {
    case 200: println("OK")
    case 404: println("Not found")
    case _: println("Unknown: {status}")
}

Coming in 1.0: range patterns

case 500..600: (half-open, as every range) and case 500..=599:.

A case can run several statements — they all belong to the case until the next case:

match (status) {
    case 200:
        log("serving")
        println("OK")
    case _:
        println("Unknown: {status}")
}

Enum variants match by their qualified name, and payload fields bind as names. A variant with a payload lists its field types:

enum Shape : int32 {
    Circle(float64)
    Rect(float64, float64)
    Empty
}

match (shape) {
    case Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
    case Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
    case Shape.Empty: return 0.0
}

docs.title: Break and continue
docs.text:
for (i in 0..<100) {
    if (i == 50) {
        break
    }
    if (i % 2 == 0) {
        continue
    }
    println("{i}")
}

docs.title: Try / catch / finally
docs.text:
throw raises an error with a message; catch receives it:

func parse_port(str s) -> int32 {
    if (s.len() == 0) {
        throw("empty port")
    }
    return 8080
}

func main() -> int32 {
    try {
        int32 p = parse_port("")
        println("{p}")
    } catch (Error e) {
        println("error: {e}")
    } finally {
        println("done")
    }
    return 0
}

The finally block always runs, whether or not an error occurred. Library functions report failures the same way: std.base64's base64_decode throws on malformed input, for example.

Coming in 1.0

Typed errors (catch (IOError e)), several catch clauses tried in order, and an error value with fields such as e.message.

docs.title: An error nobody catches
docs.text:
An error that no try catches ends the program, wherever it was thrown: in main or in any Hemerodrome (a spawned task). The program prints

stenopos: uncaught exception in a task: connect db:5432: connection refused

on stderr, flushes what it had printed, and exits with code 70. It does not carry on with one task silently gone: a server whose request handler throws stops, so a supervisor (Kubernetes, systemd) restarts it and the failure shows. To keep running, catch the error where you can handle it, for example around each request:

// docs-snippet: skip
try {
    h.respond(handle(r))
} catch (str e) {
    eprintln("request failed: " + e)
    h.respond(text(500, "internal server error\n"))
}

Library functions that wait on the network don't throw for conditions a server is expected to ride out: accept waits, with a warning, when the process has run out of file descriptors, and skips a client that gave up before it was accepted.

docs.title: With (scoped cleanup)
docs.text:
with holds a resource for a block and releases it when the block ends, on every path. Locks use it today:

mutex[int32] m = mutex(0)
with (g = m.guard()) {
    g.set(g.get() + 1)
}
// the lock is released here

Coming in 1.0

Files: with (File f = open("log.txt")) { f.write("entry\n") }.

docs.title: Defer
docs.text:
defer schedules an expression to run when its enclosing block exits — by any path: falling off the end, an early return, a break/continue, or a throw. Deferred expressions run last-in-first-out, and before the block's locals are freed, so cleanup can still use them.

func process() -> void {
    println("open")
    defer println("close")   // runs no matter how process() exits
    println("work")
    // ... "close" prints here automatically ...
}

defer is block-scoped: a defer inside a loop body fires at the end of each iteration, not all at once when the function returns.

for (i in 0..=2) {
    defer println("close {i}")
    println("open {i}")
}
// open 0 / close 0 / open 1 / close 1 / open 2 / close 2

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
@requires and @ensures attach a precondition and a postcondition to a function. Both are boolean expressions checked at run time; @ensures also sees the returned value as result. A violated contract reports which one failed and stops the program — a broken assumption halts at the boundary that stated it, instead of corrupting whatever comes next.

@requires(n >= 0)
@ensures(result >= 1)
func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
}

Several @requires may be stacked; each is checked on entry.

docs.title: Nested error handling
docs.text:
try blocks nest; an error is caught by the innermost catch around it:

try {
    try {
        throw("inner")
    } catch (Error e) {
        println("caught {e}")
        throw("outer")
    }
} catch (Error e) {
    println("then caught {e}")
}

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    return a + b
}

func greet(str name) -> void {     // `-> void` is required
    println("Hello, {name}!")
}

Return values are must-use: calling add(1, 2) and ignoring the result is a compile error. Use it, assign it, discard add(1, 2) to drop it on purpose, or mark the function @ignore_discard.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
func identity[T](T val) -> T {
    return val
}

int32 n = identity(7)
str s = identity("hi")

docs.title: Lambdas
docs.text:
A lambda's parameters and return type are written out. Its type is fn(parameter types)->return type:

fn(int32)->int32 square = |int32 n| -> int32 {
    return n * n
}

fn()->void hello = || -> void {
    println("hello")
}

func apply(fn(int32)->int32 f, int32 x) -> int32 {
    return f(x)
}

A lambda can use variables from where it's defined (captures them).

A named function is a value of its function type too, so it can be stored or passed without wrapping it in a lambda:

func square(int32 n) -> int32 {
    return n * n
}

fn(int32)->int32 f = square
int32 v = apply(square, 5)      // 25

A function type can name any parameter or return type, List and HashMap included: fn(List[int32])->int32. Lists, maps and structs are borrowed when passed through a function value, exactly as in a direct call.

Taking a function as a value needs the same @cap declarations as calling it, since the call through the value isn't checked again. Generic and extern functions can't be values; wrap one in a lambda that calls it.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Methods are written inside a struct or class, and reach the value as this:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y

    pub func norm2() -> float64 {
        return this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y
    }
}

docs.title: What the compiler checks, and what it works out
docs.text:
C compilers let you describe a function to the optimizer with attributes: GCC's pure, const, malloc, nonnull, access(read_only, ...). Those are promises the compiler trusts: mark a function const when it does read memory, and the program is silently miscompiled. Stenopos has no annotation whose mistake is undefined behaviour. Each one is one of three kinds:

Checked guarantees. You declare them; the compiler proves them, through every call, and refuses the program when they don't hold. They are part of the function's contract, and a caller relies on them.

Annotation What is guaranteed @cap(File), @cap(Network)... The function (and what it calls) uses only the capabilities it names; a caller must hold them too. @pure / @io / @net Its effects: @pure does no I/O at all, @io touches files and the console, @net the network. @no_return It never returns: a return in it is a compile error, and running off its end stops the program rather than continuing. @secret A secret value may not decide a branch (that would leak it through timing). @sensitive The value's memory is wiped when it is freed.

Hints. You declare them; they change speed or layout, never meaning, so a wrong hint costs time, not correctness: @inline, @hot, @cold, @section("name").

Inferred facts. You write nothing; the compiler works them out (whether a function allocates, which memory it reads or writes) and tells the optimizer, so you get what GCC's memory attributes give, with no way to get them wrong. Planned after 1.0, measured by the benchmark gate.

What comes next follows the same rule. @noalloc, a checked guarantee that a function and everything it calls never allocate (for interrupt handlers, real-time paths and kernel code), is designed for the kernel milestones; the memory facts above will be inferred, not declared.

docs.title: Coming in 1.0
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

These are part of the 1.0 language and are being built.

// Default parameters
func connect(str host = "localhost", int32 port = 8080) -> bool {
    return true
}

// Named arguments
connect(port: 443, host: "example.com")

// Multiple return values via tuples
func divmod(int32 a, int32 b) -> (int32, int32) {
    return (a / b, a % b)
}
(int32 q, int32 r) = divmod(17, 5)

// Methods declared outside the type
func (Point p).distance() -> float64 {
    return sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y)
}

// Functions evaluated at compile time
const func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
}
const int32 F10 = factorial(10)

docs.title: Memory Safety
docs.text: Stenopos manages memory with NOVA: no garbage collector and no manual free. The compiler inserts every allocation's release at the point the value's owner goes away.

docs.title: Freed at the end of scope
docs.text:
func process() -> void {
    str data = "a string on the heap"
    println(data)
    // data is freed here, automatically
}

Strings, lists and maps free their memory when their owner leaves scope, on every path out: falling off the end, return, break, continue or a throw. The CI runs the whole test corpus under valgrind and accepts no use-after-free, no double free and no leak.

Sending a local string, list, map or struct on a channel moves it: the receiver owns it now. Using it afterwards is a compile error until it is assigned a new value, on every path: after an if that sent it in one branch, after a loop that sent it and left with break, and in a loop that sends it and goes round again without assigning it:

func main() -> void {
    chan[str] c = chan()
    str job = "first"
    c.send(job)
    // println(job)       // error: `job` was moved: sent on a channel at line 4
    job = "second"        // a new value: usable again
    c.send(job)
}

A parameter is sent as a copy (the caller still owns it), and numbers and bool always copy. From rc.8; before, a value used after send read as empty or crashed. Moves at every hand-over (str b = a) come with M6 (ADR-0040).

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Every value has exactly one owner.

A string, list, map or struct that holds one moves when it is handed to a new owner (ADR-0040, from rc.8): str b = a, xs.push(a), storing a in a field, returning it, sending it, spawn f(a), or passing it to a function that keeps that parameter. Using a afterwards is a compile error, on every path, until a is assigned again:

func main() -> void {
    str a = "one" + "!"
    str b = a
    // println(a)          // error: `a` was moved: assigned to `b` at line 3
    a = "two"              // a new value: usable again
    println("{a} {b}")
}

Nullable strings, lists and maps (str?, List[T]?, HashMap[K, V]?) move the same way, and .clone() copies one, null or not.

A nullable struct is how linked structures are built, so a Node? local given a value that lives elsewhere (another variable, a field) is a view of it: nothing is copied, and changes through it change the structure. While a view is still read, nothing may free what it points into, which the compiler checks:

struct Node {
    int32 v
    Node? next
}

func main() -> void {
    Node? head = Node { v: 1, next: Node { v: 2, next: null } }
    Node? cur = head
    while (cur != null) {
        cur.v = cur.v * 10           // changes the list
        cur = cur.next
    }
    // head = null here, then reading cur: an error (cur would point into
    // freed memory)
    Node? copy = head.clone()        // keeping a node elsewhere: say so
    println("{copy?.v ?? 0}")
}

Storing a view (or a node read out of a field) anywhere but a local Node? (a field, a list, a return) needs .clone(). Numbers, bool and structs made only of them copy as before. Nothing is ever copied without saying so: x.clone() makes an independent deep copy, and reading a value out of a field or a list or map element into a new owner (str n = job.name, str w = words.get(0)) needs .clone() (or .take(), below) too; the compiler says which. Reading without making a new owner (printing it, .len(), comparing, passing it to a function that only reads it) copies nothing.

A function keeps a parameter when it hands it on itself (stores it, returns it, sends it, or passes it to another function that keeps it); the compiler works this out from the function's body, across the program. After keep(x), x is moved; after show(x), a function that only reads it, it isn't. c.send(job.clone()) sends a copy and keeps job.

docs.title: Loop variables
docs.text:
for (s in names) doesn't copy each element: s is a view of the element, which the list still owns. Reading it costs nothing; handing it to a new owner needs s.clone(), and changing it (assigning it, setting a field, s.items.push(..), or passing it to a function that changes it) is an error, since it would change the list:

struct P {
    str name
}

func main() -> void {
    List[P] ps = [P { name: "a" }]
    List[str] names = list_new()
    for (p in ps) {
        println(p.name)              // a read: no copy
        names.push(p.name.clone())   // a new owner: say so
        // p.name = "b"              // error: `p` is a view of the list's element
    }
}

When the loop's body changes the list it iterates (pushes to it, sets an element, passes it to a function that changes it), each element is copied instead, so the loop variable never points into memory the change moved.

Code written before rc.8 can be migrated: STENOPOS_MOVES=report stenopos build ... prints, instead of each error, a warning naming the token after which .clone() keeps the old behaviour.

xs.remove(i) takes an element out of a list (closing the gap), and m.remove(k) takes a value out of a map (null when the key is absent): the caller owns what comes out, and nothing is copied.

x.take() moves a string, list or map out of a variable or a field without copying it, and leaves an empty one in its place: str name = job.name.take(). Nothing of the value stays behind, so it is the way to hand on a secret. Clone when you want two copies; take when you want the value somewhere else and none left behind. Freed memory can be wiped too: see Wiping freed memory.

docs.title: Secrets stay out of the stack, swap and core dumps
docs.text:
A value marked @sensitive (or of a secret[T] type) is protected wherever the language can protect it (from rc.8):

  • Freed: its bytes are zeroed first.
  • Swap: while a @sensitive variable holds a value, the pages that hold its bytes are locked in RAM, so the system never writes them to swap. They are unlocked when the variable lets go. Locking is limited by the system's RLIMIT_MEMLOCK (ulimit -l); past it, a page stays unlocked.
  • Core dumps: a program that has any secret turns its own core dumps off when it starts, and on Linux other users' debuggers can't attach to it, so no copy of a secret, a temporary one included, reaches a dump file.
  • The stack: after calling a function that holds a secret, the caller zeroes the stack below it, which removes the callee's locals, the copies the compiler spilled there and everything the callee's own callees left.

What no language can do is erase a file: on SSDs and journaling file systems, deleting or overwriting it doesn't reliably remove the old bytes. Store secrets encrypted instead.

docs.title: Parameters borrow
docs.text:
Passing a struct, list or map to a function doesn't copy it: the parameter borrows the caller's value for the length of the call. A function that changes its parameter changes the caller's value, just as a method changes this:

struct Account {
    str owner
    float64 balance
}

func transfer(Account from, Account to, float64 amount) -> void {
    from.balance = from.balance - amount
    to.balance = to.balance + amount
}

func main() -> void {
    Account a = Account { owner: "ana", balance: 100.0 }
    Account b = Account { owner: "ben", balance: 0.0 }
    transfer(a, b, 30.0)
    println("{a.balance} {b.balance}")   // 70 30
}

Assigning to the parameter itself (from = Account { ... }) only rebinds the name inside the function; the caller's value is untouched. Returning a parameter returns a copy.

A value passed to a parameter the function changes can't also appear in another argument of the same call: both parameters would name the same value, and a push through one could move the memory the other is reading. The compiler works out which parameters each function changes (following the calls it makes), and rejects the call:

transfer(a, a, 30.0)
// error: `a` is passed to `transfer` twice, and `transfer` changes its
// parameter `from`, so two parameters would borrow the same value; pass
// a copy instead: `Account a_copy = a`

The same goes for a value and a field inside it (f(a, a.items)) and for a method's receiver (a.merge(a)). Strings and numbers are passed by value, so they never conflict. spawn gives the new Hemerodrome its own copy of each struct argument, because it can outlive the caller.

Coming in 1.0: moves (ADR-0040)

Values that own heap memory (str, List, HashMap, and structs that contain them) will move instead: after str b = a, a can no longer be used, and the compiler reports it if you try. Copying becomes explicit with .clone(). Numbers, bool and structs of plain data still copy implicitly. A parameter keeps borrowing (above) unless the function keeps the value, by storing or returning it: then the parameter consumes it, with no copy. The compiler infers this without any annotation, as it already infers which parameters are changed. spawn takes its arguments instead of copying them, and a clone of a @sensitive or secret value stays protected.

str a = "hello"
str b = a          // a moves into b
println(a)         // error: use of moved value `a`
str c = b.clone()  // an explicit, independent copy

Moves make transfers free (no hidden copies), let messages and channels hand data over without copying, and let capabilities be values that can't be duplicated.

docs.title: Raw pointers
docs.text:
For talking to C, raw pointers exist, confined to unsafe blocks:

func main() -> void {
    int32 x = 41
    unsafe {
        ptr[int32] p = &x
        *p = *p + 1
    }
    println("{x}")     // 42
}

Everything that makes or uses a pointer needs unsafe (ADR-0041): taking an address (&x), reading or writing through one (*p), casting to or from one, comparing two, and calling a C function. So the unsafe blocks are the complete list of places to audit.

A ptr[T] knows its T: *p reads and writes a T, and a ptr[int64] isn't a ptr[int32]. ptr[void] is C's void *: any pointer converts to it, and it converts back only by a cast. C's narrow integers (uint8, int8, uint16, int16) have no Stenopos type of their own: through a ptr[uint8], *p reads an int32 and a store keeps the low byte. &s of a struct is the address of its fields, which is what C's struct T * means.

extern "C" {
    func malloc(uint64 size) -> ptr[void]
    func free(ptr[void] p) -> void
}

func main() -> void {
    unsafe {
        ptr[int64] p = cast[ptr[int64]](malloc(8))     // ptr[void] -> ptr[int64]
        if (p != cast[ptr[int64]](0)) {                 // null is cast[ptr[T]](0)
            *p = 5000000000
            println("{*p} at {cast[uint64](p)}")       // an address is a uint64
            free(p)
        }
    }
}

A device register is memory that acts: writing a UART's data register sends a byte, and its status register changes on its own. volatile_read(p) and volatile_write(p, v) are *p and *p = v that the compiler performs exactly as written, once each and in order, even when nothing reads the value back (which would otherwise let the optimizer drop the write):

func put(uint8 c) -> void {
    unsafe {
        ptr[uint8] status = cast[ptr[uint8]](cast[uint64](0x10000005))
        while ((volatile_read(status) & 32) == 0) {      // wait until it can send
        }
        volatile_write(cast[ptr[uint8]](cast[uint64](0x10000000)), c)
    }
}

Volatile keeps the compiler's order, not the processor's: for that, see fences.

From rc.8; in rc.7 and earlier &x was allowed outside unsafe, *p read an int32 whatever T was, and there was no volatile access. Reading a whole struct through a pointer (*p on a ptr[S]) isn't supported yet: pass the pointer on to C.

docs.title: Device registers
docs.text:
Raw addresses, widths and casts repeated through every driver are where a wrong offset hides. A register block describes a device's registers once, by offset, width and access (ADR-0058):

@registers
struct Ns16550 {
    @at(0x0) write uint8 thr      // transmit holding: a byte written is sent
    @at(0x1) uint8 ier            // interrupt enable: read and written
    @at(0x5) read uint8 lsr       // line status: bit 5, ready for a byte
}

func uart() -> Ns16550 {
    unsafe {
        return registers_at[Ns16550](0x10000000)   // the one unsafe fact
    }
}

func put(Ns16550 u, uint8 c) -> void {
    while ((u.lsr & 32) == 0) {          // one volatile 8-bit read per test
    }
    u.thr = c                            // one volatile 8-bit write
}
  • @at(offset) places each register, in bytes from the block's address. A register is uint8, uint16, uint32 or uint64; registers may leave gaps, but may not overlap and must be aligned to their width.
  • read or write restricts a register; no keyword means both. Reading a write register or writing a read one is a compile error naming it, and so is += on a write register (it would read first).
  • Every access is exactly one volatile access of the register's width, as volatile_read and volatile_write are. A read-modify-write is written out (u.ier = u.ier + 1): two accesses, both visible.
  • registers_at[T](address) binds a block to an address, inside unsafe: nothing can check that the device is there. After that, accesses need no unsafe. A block's value is its address: passing it, returning it, or holding it in a struct copies the address, never the device.

In a firmware project the addresses aren't in the source at all: Tagma.toml's [devices] binds each block, and main receives the board (func main(Board board), then board.uart0), with no unsafe; see Firmware.

From rc.8. Still to come: making a bound block move-only, so one driver owns a device (with move checking, M6); bit fields by name; and register arrays.

docs.title: Interrupts, statics and fences
docs.text:
A timer's interrupt arrives between any two instructions; the code it runs needs somewhere to keep what it counts, and a driver handing a buffer to a device needs memory to settle in order. Three things cover it (ADR-0059).

Statics. A static is a variable that lives for the whole program, declared at the top of a module: an integer, bool or float64, with a constant first value. Reading or writing one is unsafe, since an interrupt can change it between two instructions and nothing makes that safe until M6's atomics. Every access is volatile, so a loop waiting for an interrupt reads it each time round:

static uint64 ticks = 0

func tick() -> void {
    unsafe {
        ticks += 1
    }
}

func main() -> void {
    tick()
    tick()
    unsafe {
        println("{ticks} ticks")      // 2 ticks
    }
}

A local of the same name hides a static. A pub static can be imported from another module like a function.

Interrupt handlers. @interrupt marks a function the hardware runs: no result, and no parameters or, as main does, the Board, so a timer's handler can re-arm its timer. It is ordinary, checked Stenopos. The compiler writes its entry, which saves the registers the handler may change (the FP/SIMD state too when the board uses its FPU: see float64 on a board), calls it, restores them and returns from the exception (mret, eret, iretq). interrupt_entry(f) is the entry's address, a uint64, for the board's code to install: in mtvec on RISC-V, as a branch in the vector table on ARM64, in an IDT gate on x86-64. On RISC-V (QEMU's virt board):

@interrupt
func on_timer(Board board) -> void {
    unsafe {
        ticks += 1
    }
    arm(board.clint, 100000)         // the next one in 10 ms
}

func take_ticks(Board board) -> void {
    uint64 entry = interrupt_entry(on_timer)
    arm(board.clint, 100000)
    unsafe {
        asm {
            "csrw mtvec, %0"         // interrupts run on_timer's entry
            "li t0, 0x80"
            "csrs mie, t0"           // the timer's interrupt
            "csrsi mstatus, 0x8"     // interrupts on
            :
            : "r"(entry)
            : "t0"
        }
    }
}

@interrupt is for freestanding programs. The interrupt controller (acknowledging, priorities, nesting) is the program's, written with register blocks; stenopos-os's pathfinder takes timer interrupts this way on RISC-V, ARM64 (the GIC) and x86-64 (the local APIC). An x86-64 board build leaves out the red zone, since an interrupt pushes its frame just below the stack pointer.

Fences. memory_fence() makes every memory access before it, to memory or a device, complete before any after it begins, as the whole system sees it (fence iorw, iorw on RISC-V, dsb sy on ARM64, mfence on x86-64). Volatile access keeps the compiler's order; a fence keeps the processor's and the bus's, for instance between filling a buffer and telling a device to read it. It is safe code. There is one fence, the strongest; lighter ones can come when a measurement asks for them.

From rc.8. Still to come with M6: atomics, so a counter shared with a handler needs no unsafe.

docs.title: Calling C
docs.text:
extern "C" {
    func abs(int32 n) -> int32
    func labs(int64 n) -> int64
}

func main() -> void {
    unsafe {
        println("{abs(0 - 7)} {labs(0 - 9)}")
    }
}

From rc.8 a C function can take and return any of these, mixed freely, and each call's arguments are checked against them like any other call's:

Stenopos C int32, uint32 int, unsigned int64, uint64 long, size_t (and other 64-bit integers) bool bool (_Bool, one byte) float64 double ptr[T] T * (a struct with @repr("C"), or a scalar) str (parameters) const char *: a NUL-terminated copy, valid for the call 
extern "C" {
    func strlen(str s) -> uint64
    func snprintf(ptr[uint8] buf, uint64 size, str fmt, ...) -> int32
}

A str with a NUL byte inside stops the program rather than reaching C: C would read only up to the NUL, and a path or a name cut short is a bug at best. A C function can't return str (who frees C's string is up to C): return ptr[uint8] and copy it. After ..., a variadic function's arguments travel as C's default promotions do. Integer literals, and arithmetic on them (0 - 7), take the parameter's type; an int32 variable does not become an int64 without cast[int64]().

Structs by value. A @repr("C") struct whose fields are scalars, pointers or enums can be a C function's parameter or result. How C passes structs differs on every architecture, so the call goes through a small C wrapper that the compiler writes and the target's own C compiler builds:

@repr("C")
struct DivT {
    int32 quot
    int32 rem
}

extern "C" func div(int32 num, int32 den) -> DivT

Callbacks. A parameter of a function type takes a named top-level function, which C calls through a plain function pointer:

extern "C" func qsort(ptr[int32] base, uint64 n, uint64 size, fn(ptr[int32], ptr[int32]) -> int32 compare) -> void

Its parameters and result must be ones C can pass (integers, float64, bool and pointers), and a lambda isn't accepted: its captured variables have no C form. An error thrown out of a callback can't unwind through C's frames, so it ends the program (exit status 70) with its message.

Limits today

rc.7 and earlier: parameters and result all int32, or all int64, and none of the above. Still to come: a struct whose field is another struct is stored as a pointer to it, not inline as C stores it, so such a struct can't be passed by value yet, and reading one through a pointer isn't C's layout.

docs.title: No null dereferences
docs.text: Nullable values (T?) must be checked before use; the compiler narrows the type after the check (see Variables and Types). Raw pointers will follow the same rule as ptr[T]?.

docs.title: Declaring a module
docs.text: module math.vector

docs.title: Visibility: pub vs. private
docs.text:
Declarations are private to their module by default. A function, struct, enum, trait, type alias or top-level const is only visible to code in the same module unless you mark it pub. Reaching for a private name from another module is a compile error:

module math.internal

pub func cube(int32 n) -> int32 {   // public API — callable anywhere
    return n * square(n)
}

func square(int32 n) -> int32 {     // private — only this module may use it
    return n * n
}

module app.main

import math.internal.{cube}

func main() -> void {
    println("{cube(3)}")            // ok — cube is pub
    // println("{square(3)}")       // compile error: square is private to math.internal
}

This keeps a module's surface area deliberate: callers depend only on what you chose to expose, and you can refactor everything else freely.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
Name what you use from a module:

import math.vector.{Vec3, Vec4}   // several names
import math.vector.Vec3           // one name, without braces
import math.vector.*              // every public name
import math.vector                // the whole module: `vector.Vec3`

* brings in only pub names; a private one stays private however it is imported.

docs.title: Qualified names
docs.text:
A module imported whole qualifies its names with its last segment, so two modules' items of the same name can be used side by side:

import geo.flat
import geo.round

flat.Point a = flat.make(1, 2)
round.Point b = round.Point { r: 5 }
flat.Side s = flat.Side.Right
println("{flat.ORIGIN_X}")

In the importing module the qualifier names only the module: a variable or parameter called flat is an error there. Importing a module whole also brings in its methods on built-in types (import std.string).

docs.title: Renaming with as
docs.text:
as gives an imported item, or a module's qualifier, another name:

import geo.round as r                     // r.Point, r.describe(...)
import geo.flat.describe as describe_flat
import geo.{Point as GeoPoint, distance}

The item is then imported only under the new name. Two modules imported whole under the same qualifier are an error; rename one with as.

docs.title: Which import wins
docs.text:
A module's own items come first, then names imported explicitly, then names offered by *:

import geo.a.*
import geo.b.*
import geo.b.helper     // `helper` is geo.b's, though geo.a.* offers one too

When two * imports offer different items under one name, using that name is an error until you import the one you mean by name. Importing one name explicitly from two modules is an error too. A clash you never use costs nothing, and the same item reached by two paths (directly and through a re-export) is one item, not a clash.

error[E0300]: `helper` is ambiguous: `geo.a.*` and `geo.b.*` both offer it;
import the one you mean by name (`import geo.a.helper`)

The compiler finds a module by its module line, in the project's own files, its dependencies (see tagma) and the standard library.

docs.title: Relative imports
docs.text:
A path may start from the importing module: self is the module itself and super its parent (super.super the grandparent).

module app.net

import self.http.{Request}     // app.net.http
import super.config.*          // app.config

docs.title: Re-exports
docs.text:
pub import makes imported names part of this module's own public surface, so a facade module can present items that live in submodules:

module geo

pub import self.core.{Point, distance}
pub import self.units.*
pub import self.flat.{make as flat_point}   // re-exported under another name

module app

import geo.{Point, distance}    // defined in geo.core, offered by geo

A re-export names items (or *); pub import of a whole module is an error.

docs.title: Example layout
docs.text:
src/
  main.sten          module app
  math/
    vector.sten      module math.vector
    matrix.sten      module math.matrix

A module may live in any file; its module line names it. Keeping the path and the module name in step makes a project easy to navigate.

docs.title: Language Guide Overview
docs.text: Stenopos is a statically typed systems language with C-style brace syntax and no semicolons. This guide walks through the core language features.

docs.title: Design goals
docs.text:
• Readable — curly-brace blocks, no semicolons
  • Safe by default — memory safety, taint tracking, effect types built into the type system
  • C-compatible — call C libraries directly (extern "C")
  • One toolchain — tagma builds, runs, tests, formats and lints projects; stenopos, the compiler, does the same for single files
