docs.title: Writing a service
docs.text: A service is a program that runs until it is told to stop: it answers requests, does work in the background, and finishes cleanly when Kubernetes (or systemd, or Ctrl-C) says so. This page builds one and explains each part. Everything here is in the standard library from rc.7.

docs.title: The whole service
docs.text:
An HTTP endpoint that queues jobs, a worker that does them one at a time, health probes, and a clean stop on SIGTERM:

import std.net.{Conn, Listener, listen, accept, close}
import std.http.{Request, HttpConn, serve, limits, text, json}
import std.os.{notify_signals, exit, SIGTERM, SIGINT}
import std.time.{sleep_ms, rfc3339, unix}

// One connection: requests until the client is done.
@cap(Network)
func handle(Conn c, chan[str] jobs) -> void {
    HttpConn h = serve(c, limits())
    bool open = true
    while (open) {
        Request? got = h.next()
        if (got == null) {
            open = false
        } else {
            Request r = got!!
            if (r.path == "/healthz" || r.path == "/readyz") {
                h.respond(text(200, "ok\n"))
            } else if (r.path == "/jobs" && r.method == "POST") {
                jobs.send(r.body)
                h.respond(json(202, "\{\"queued\": true\}"))
            } else {
                h.respond(text(404, "not found\n"))
            }
        }
    }
    discard close(c)
}

@cap(Network)
func http_server(Listener l, chan[str] jobs) -> void {
    while (true) {
        spawn handle(accept(l), jobs)
    }
}

// The work: one job at a time, a heartbeat when idle.
func worker(chan[str] jobs, chan[str] done) -> void {
    while (true) {
        str? job = jobs.recv_timeout(10000)
        if (job == null) {
            println(rfc3339(unix()) + " idle")
        } else {
            sleep_ms(50)                       // the job's real work goes here
            done.send(job!!)
        }
    }
}

@cap(Network)
@cap(Process)
func main() -> void {
    chan[int32] stop = chan()
    notify_signals([SIGTERM, SIGINT], stop)
    chan[str] jobs = chan()
    chan[str] done = chan()
    spawn http_server(listen(8080), jobs)
    spawn worker(jobs, done)
    println("listening on :8080")
    bool running = true
    while (running) {
        str? finished = done.recv_timeout(1000)
        if (finished != null) {
            println("done: " + finished!!)
        }
        if (stop.try_recv() != null) {
            running = false
        }
    }
    println("stopping")
    exit(0)
}

tagma run
curl localhost:8080/healthz                  # ok
curl -d 'resize photo 1' localhost:8080/jobs # {"queued": true}
kill -TERM <pid>                             # stopping

docs.title: Tasks and channels
docs.text:
Each spawn starts a Hemerodrome, a lightweight task. Thousands are cheap. Tasks share nothing by default: they hand values to each other over channels (chan[T]), and a value sent is moved, so only one task owns it at a time.

A task that waits (on a socket, a timer, a channel, a child process or a signal) parks: its worker thread runs the other tasks meanwhile. That is why the server, the worker and main above can all wait at once, even on a machine with one CPU.

Waiting is always bounded when you want it to be:

Wait Forever With a deadline Without waiting A channel c.recv() c.recv_timeout(ms) → T? c.try_recv() → T? A socket recv(conn) recv_timeout(conn, ms) → str? poll(conns, 0) A connection connect(host, port) connect_timeout(host, port, ms) Time sleep_ms(ms)

null means "nothing arrived in time"; the empty string from a socket means the peer closed it.

A function can start a task and hand back its channel:

func start_worker() -> chan[str] {
    chan[str] jobs = chan()
    spawn worker(jobs)
    return jobs                 // the caller owns it; the worker keeps running
}

Channels, locks, semaphores and atomics are reference counted (from rc.8): the scope that creates one holds a reference, and so does each task it is given to. A function's end lets go of its reference and never waits: the handle lives on while a task still holds it. (In rc.7 such a function waited for every task in the program, so a request handler that made a channel for its own use hung in a service; ADR-0045.) Only the end of main waits for tasks.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
std.http serves one connection per task. serve(conn, limits()) reads requests (keep-alive included) and answers malformed or oversized ones itself: 400, 431 for headers over 16 KiB, 413 for bodies over 1 MiB, and a client silent for 10 s is dropped. Change limits()'s fields to change those. next() returns null when the client is done.

The 10 s is per read, not per request: a client that trickles one byte at a time can keep a connection open far longer, and nothing yet caps how many connections are open at once. On the public internet, run the service behind a proxy or load balancer that enforces both. Deadlines for the header block and the body, and a connection cap, are planned.

A handler that throws ends the whole program (an error nobody catches): catch errors around each request when one bad request shouldn't stop the service.

The client is a separate module, std.http.client, so a server that never makes requests doesn't link OpenSSL:

import std.http.client.{ClientRequest, request, get, post_json, fetch}
import std.tls.{pinned}

Response r = get("https://gitea.example.com/api/v1/version")
Response p = post_json("http://localhost:8080/jobs", "\{\"id\": 1\}")
ClientRequest q = request("GET", "https://10.0.0.1/api/self")
q.tls = pinned("5f:3a:...")             // a device with a self-signed certificate
q.headers.push("Cookie: TOKEN=...")
q.timeout_ms = 5000
Response s = fetch(q)

A failure (refused, timed out, an untrusted certificate) throws, saying why; an HTTP error status is just a Response with that status.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
std.tls uses the system's OpenSSL, linked into programs that use std.tls or std.http.client, so their image needs libssl3 (it comes with ca-certificates); a program that uses neither doesn't. It speaks TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. There are two ways to trust a server, and checking nothing is refused:

  • verified(): the certificate chains to a trusted CA (the system's, or ca_file) and names the host.
  • pinned(sha256): exactly this certificate, as openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 prints it. For devices with self-signed certificates. A wrong pin fails before anything is sent.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits (30 s by default), then sends SIGKILL. Deliver signals into a channel and finish what you are doing:

chan[int32] stop = chan()
notify_signals([SIGTERM, SIGINT], stop)
// ... in the main loop:
if (stop.try_recv() != null) {
    running = false
}

Then end with exit(0). Returning from main waits for every task, so work a program started is always finished, never cut off. A service's accept loop never finishes, so a service ends with exit(code), which flushes output and stops the tasks: each worker gets up to 1 s to reach a point where it can stop. If a program does return from main and is still waiting after 3 s, it says so on stderr, with the way out.

exit_grace(ms) sets a limit for that wait: past it, the program says which wait ran out and exits with 124. A batch job leaves it unset, so its work always finishes; a service might set exit_grace(25000), inside Kubernetes's 30 s.

docs.title: Files and logs
docs.text:
std.fs does what a shell would, without a shell: read (null when the file is missing), write_atomic (a reader never sees half a file), append, list_dir, stat, mkdir_all, rename, remove_all, temp_dir, chmod, set_umask. std.logging writes leveled records to the console or a file; a file logger appends each record in one write, so tasks logging at once never lose lines.

For programs, std.os.execute(["tar", "-czf", out, dir]) runs one without a shell and returns its exit code, stdout and stderr: nothing in an argument is ever interpreted.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Every function that touches the outside world says so: @cap(Network), @cap(File), @cap(Process). main above declares Network and Process; the compiler refuses a function that uses a capability it doesn't declare, so tagma caps lists exactly what a service can do, and a dependency gets only the capabilities its allow grants it.

docs.title: Building and running it in a container
docs.text:
tagma build --release                     # target/release/<name>, stripped and hardened

FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*           # libssl3 for std.tls comes with it
COPY target/release/myservice /usr/local/bin/myservice
USER 65534
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/myservice"]

The binary needs only the C library (and libssl if it uses std.tls or std.http.client). Its output is flushed line by line when it goes to a pipe or a terminal, so kubectl logs shows each line as it is printed. Point Kubernetes's probes at /healthz and /readyz.

To keep a log of builds, add [output] log = "logs/build.log" to Tagma.toml (where tagma's messages go).

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Plain data containers:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y
}

Point p = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }
println("{p.x}, {p.y}")

A type is used below its declaration: a function can be called before it is declared, but a struct, class or enum must come first in the file (or be imported). Using a type that isn't declared yet, or at all, is an error naming it, wherever it appears: a variable, parameter, result, field, cast or trait signature. (Before rc.8 some of those positions quietly read an unknown name as int32.)

Structs and classes can have methods, which reach the value as this:

struct Point {
    float64 x
    float64 y

    pub func norm2() -> float64 {
        return this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y
    }
}

A type's methods are written inside it, and only there: impl is for implementing a trait (below). A separate impl Point { ... } block is an error that says where the methods go (ADR-0044 D7, from rc.8).

docs.title: Generic structs
docs.text:
struct Pair[A, B] {
    A first
    B second
}

Pair[int32, str] p = Pair { first: 7, second: "seven" }

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Classes add inheritance. Like structs, they are values: a class instance lives where its variable lives, with no hidden heap allocation and no garbage collector.

class Animal {
    pub str name

    virtual func speak() -> void {
        println("...")
    }
}

class Dog : Animal {
    override func speak() -> void {
        println("Woof! I'm {this.name}")
    }
}

Use parent to call the parent class method:

class Puppy : Dog {
    override func speak() -> void {
        parent.speak()
        println("*wags tail*")
    }
}

A derived value is never silently converted to its base type (that would drop its fields). For polymorphism, use dyn:

class Shape {
    virtual func name() -> str {
        return "shape"
    }
}

class Square : Shape {
    override func name() -> str {
        return "square"
    }
}

Square sq = Square {}
dyn Shape s = sq
println(s.name())        // square

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
Fields and methods are private by default: only code in their module may use them. pub makes them visible everywhere. In a class, protected opens a member to the methods of the class and its subclasses, in any module, as well as to its own module.

module bank.core

pub class Account {
    pub str owner                   // anyone
    protected float64 balance       // Account, its subclasses, bank.core

    pub func deposit(float64 amount) -> void {
        balance += amount
    }

    protected func fee() -> float64 {
        return 2.0
    }
}

module app

import bank.core.{Account}

pub class Savings : Account {
    pub func charge() -> void {
        balance -= fee()            // ok: a subclass method
    }
}

func peek(Account a) -> float64 {
    return a.balance                // error: `balance` is protected
}

A struct literal of a class declared in the current module may set every field, inherited ones too: it is how that class is constructed. protected is only for class members; a struct's members and top-level items are pub or private.

docs.title: Fields and methods without this.
docs.text: Inside a method, a field or method of the class may be named on its own: balance is this.balance and fee() is this.fee(). A local variable or parameter of the same name wins over the field (write this.rate = rate to set the field from a parameter called rate), and the class's method wins over a free function of the same name.

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
trait Describe {
    func describe() -> str
}

impl Describe for Point {
    func describe() -> str {
        return "({this.x}, {this.y})"
    }
}

A trait object, dyn Describe, holds any value whose type implements the trait:

dyn Describe d = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }
println(d.describe())

Traits can be implemented for types you didn't write, including primitives.

docs.title: Coming in 1.0
docs.text:
Not implemented yet

  • Abstract methods: abstract func area() -> float64 in a class, which every subclass must override.
  • clone(), a deep copy (part of ownership and moves).
  • Calling a void method through dyn, methods with arguments through dyn, and passing a concrete value where a dyn parameter is expected.

docs.title: Statements & Line Breaks
docs.text:
Stenopos uses newline as the statement terminator — like Go, and unlike C. There are no semicolons. Write one statement per line:

int32 x = 42
int32 y = x + 1
println("{y}")

Blank lines are ignored, so use them freely to group code. Indentation is not significant (blocks are delimited by braces), but 4-space indentation is the convention.

docs.title: Breaking a long line
docs.text: A newline ends a statement only when the line so far could be a complete statement, and the next line couldn't start one. In the three situations below the newline is treated as a space and the statement continues. There is no line-continuation character (a \ is not special here).

docs.title: 1. After an operator that needs a right-hand side
docs.text:
A line that ends on an operator which cannot finish a statement — a binary, comparison, logical, bitwise, or assignment operator, ??, a trailing ., or -> — continues onto the next line:

int32 total = first_value +
              second_value +
              third_value

if (ready &&
    count > 0) {
    // ...
}

docs.title: 2. Before an operator that can't start a statement
docs.text:
A line that starts with such an operator — +, /, %, a comparison, &&, ||, ^, <<, >>, ??, . or ?. — continues the line above. This is the natural way to break a long expression or a method chain:

str message = "backup "
    + name
    + " finished"

str result = name
    .trim()
    .to_upper()

A line starting with -, * or & begins a new statement, since one can (-n is an expression, *p = 3 a store). Break those after the operator instead. A blank line, or a line holding only a comment, ends the statement.

docs.title: 3. Inside brackets ( … ) and [ … ]
docs.text:
Newlines between a matching (/) or [/] are ignored, so call arguments, function parameters, array/list literals, and parenthesized expressions may span lines:

int32 s = add(
    add(1, 2),
    add(3, 4))

func distance(float64 x,
              float64 y) -> float64 {
    return x * x + y * y
}

int32[3] triple = [10,
                   20,
                   30]

No trailing comma

Close the list right after the last element (3) above, not 3,)). A trailing comma before the closing bracket is a syntax error.

docs.title: String interpolation
docs.text:
Inside an interpolated string, "{ ... }" holds an expression that is evaluated and formatted in place. The whole string literal stays on a single source line:

str name = "Stenopos"
println("Hello, {name}! 1 + 1 = {1 + 1}")

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: You want to… Do this End a statement Start a new line (no ;) Continue a long expression End the line on an operator (+, &&, =, a trailing ., …) — it carries to the next line Spread call args / parameters / a list literal Break after a comma inside (…) or […] — no trailing comma Group code visually Use blank lines (ignored)

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
Variables are declared with the type before the name — C style, not Rust style.

int32 x = 42
int64 big = 1000000
float64 pi = 3.14159
str greeting = "hello"
bool flag = true

docs.title: Mutable by default
docs.text:
All variables are mutable. Use const to make something immutable:

const int32 MAX = 100
int32 counter = 0
counter = counter + 1   // ok
// MAX = 200            // compile error

A const outside any function belongs to its module: every function in the module can use it, above or below the declaration, as with functions (from rc.8; earlier releases need the const above its first use). Its value must be a literal, and pub const shares it with modules that import it.

docs.title: String literals
docs.text:
A string is UTF-8 text in double quotes. {expr} inside one is an interpolation: the expression's value, converted to text. A string may span lines; its newlines are part of it.

str name = "Ada"
println("Hello, {name}! {2 + 3} unread")
Escape Means \n \t \r newline, tab, carriage return \0 a NUL byte \\ \" \' a backslash, a double quote, a single quote \{ \} literal braces (not an interpolation) \xNN the byte NN, two hex digits: "\x1b[0m" (from rc.7) \u{H} the Unicode character H, 1 to 6 hex digits, as UTF-8: "caf\u{e9}" (from rc.7)

Any other escape is an error (from rc.7; earlier releases dropped the backslash). Inside { } you write code, not string text, so a string there takes plain quotes: "{m.get("a")}", never \".

A character literal in single quotes, 'a' or '\n', is one byte (an int32): '\x41' and '\u{7a}' work, '\u{e9}' (two bytes) does not.

docs.title: Comparing strings
docs.text: == and != compare strings by content, and <, <=, >, >= order them byte by byte, the way C's strcmp and Go do: "apple" < "banana", a prefix sorts first ("ab" < "abc"), and uppercase sorts before lowercase ("Zed" < "apple"). Dates written YYYY-MM-DD compare correctly as strings.

docs.title: Numeric types
docs.text:
Type Size Range int8 8-bit signed -128 to 127 int16 16-bit signed -32768 to 32767 int32 32-bit signed -2^31 to 2^31-1 int64 64-bit signed -2^63 to 2^63-1 uint8 8-bit unsigned 0 to 255 uint16 16-bit unsigned 0 to 65535 uint32 32-bit unsigned 0 to 2^32-1 uint64 64-bit unsigned 0 to 2^64-1 float64 64-bit float IEEE 754

The 8- and 16-bit integers are from rc.8 (earlier releases reserve the names). They are for data whose width is fixed outside the program: device registers, C's uint8_t and kin, and packed layouts. Their arithmetic is checked at their own width (uint8 x = 255 then x + 1 is an overflow), a literal must fit (uint8 b = 300 is an error), and they convert to other integers with cast (to float64 through int32). A list or map of them isn't supported yet. float32 is reserved for later.

Unsigned types are unsigned everywhere: comparison, /, % and >> treat the top bit as part of the value. An unsigned value can't be negated, and going below zero is an overflow.

Integer literals can be written in decimal, hex (0x) or binary (0b), and hex and binary may use _ to group digits (_ in decimal literals is coming in 1.0). A literal takes the type of the integer it is used with:

func main() -> int32 {
    uint64 mask = 0xffff_ffff_0000_0000
    uint32 flags = 0b1010
    println("{mask >> 32} {flags % 4}")
    return 0
}

An integer widens by itself to a type that holds every one of its values (ADR-0044 D3): int32 to int64, uint32 to uint64 or int64, uint8 to uint16, int32 and the rest, in assignments, arguments, returns, arithmetic and comparisons. Nothing else converts implicitly: not narrowing, not between signed and unsigned of one width, not between integers and float64. Use cast[T]() for those:

func main() -> int32 {
    List[str] words = ["one", "two", "three"]
    int32 i = 0
    while (i < words.len()) {       // i widens to int64, as len() is
        i += 1
    }
    int64 total = i                 // widening: no cast
    int32 back = cast[int32](total) // narrowing: a cast
    uint32 u = 7
    println("{total} {back} {total + u} {cast[int32](u) + i}")
    return 0
}

From rc.8; before, every conversion took a cast.

docs.title: Integer overflow is checked
docs.text:
Arithmetic that overflows its type is a bug — and a frequent source of security holes, where a wrapped size calculation leads to an undersized buffer. Stenopos does not let it happen silently. Every +, -, and * on an integer (signed or unsigned) is checked; if the result does not fit the type, the program stops with a diagnostic instead of wrapping to a wrong value:

int32 x = 2147483647    // int32 max
int32 y = x + 1         // aborts: "integer overflow: add of two int32 values"

This applies to compound assignments (+=, -=, *=) too. In-range arithmetic is unaffected, and the check is cheap — it compiles to an add plus a jump-on-overflow, not a software division.

docs.title: Opting out: wrapping_*
docs.text:
Some algorithms want modular arithmetic — hashes, checksums, PRNGs, ring-buffer indices. For those, ask for wrapping explicitly with wrapping_add, wrapping_sub, and wrapping_mul:

// FNV-1a hash — defined in terms of wrapping arithmetic, so it says so.
func fnv1a(str s) -> uint32 {
    uint32 hash = 2166136261
    int64 i = 0
    while (i < s.len()) {
        hash = wrapping_mul(hash, 16777619)
        hash = wrapping_add(hash, cast[uint32](s.byte_at(i)))
        i += 1
    }
    return hash
}

The default is safe; wrapping is opt-in and visible at the call site.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
int64[5] numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
int64 first = numbers[0]

Every index is bounds-checked: an index out of range stops the program instead of reading or writing memory it shouldn't. The C-style declaration int64 numbers[5] = ... is coming in 1.0.

docs.title: Nullable types
docs.text:
Any type T has a nullable form T? that holds either a value or null. The compiler will not let you use a T? as a T until you have ruled out null.

int32? maybe = null
str? name = "Stenopos"

Compare against null with == / !=. After a check, the value is narrowed to the non-nullable type for the rest of that scope:

func classify(int32? n) -> str {
    if (n == null) {
        return "none"
    }
    // n is narrowed to plain int32 here
    return "value: {n}"
}

Narrowing also follows && and ||: the right side of x != null && ... only runs when x isn't null, and the right side of x == null || ... only when it isn't either, so both see x as non-null. An if whose condition is such a chain narrows its branches the same way:

if (port != null && port > 1024) {
    listen(port)
}
if (a == null || b == null) {
    return 0
}
return a + b        // both narrowed: the `if` returned otherwise

Three operators work on nullables:

int32? missing = null
int32 x = missing ?? 0          // ?? — fallback when the left side is null
int32? forced = 7
int32 y = forced!!              // !! — assert non-null (aborts at runtime if null)
int64 len = name?.len() ?? 0    // ?. — safe access, yields a nullable

?? evaluates its right side only when the left side is null, so a default can be a call: cached ?? load() loads only on a miss. Fallbacks chain, tried left to right, and the chain ends with a value that can't be null:

str shown = nickname ?? full_name ?? "anonymous"

The left side of ?? must be able to be null. After if (n == null) { ... } returns, n is known not to be null, so n ?? 0 is an error: write n.

There is no null-pointer dereference: raw pointers are nullable with the same ptr[T]? syntax and must be checked before use inside unsafe.

docs.title: Type aliases
docs.text:
A type alias gives a type a second name. It is declared at the top level of a module:

type Meters = float64
type Scores = List[float64]
type Index[V] = HashMap[str, V]     // a generic alias
type MaybeId = uint64?

Meters distance = 100.0
Index[int32] ages = map_new()

An alias is transparent: Meters is float64, so a Meters passes anywhere a float64 is expected and back, with no cast. Use an alias to make a signature readable; when two quantities must not mix (metres and seconds), use a struct with one field instead, which the compiler keeps distinct.

Like other declarations, an alias is private to its module unless it is pub type, and another module imports it by name: import geo.{Meters}. An alias that refers to itself (directly or through another alias), a use with the wrong number of type arguments, and a right side that is not a type are compile errors.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Seven keywords: spawn chan atomic mutex rwlock spinlock semaphore.

spawn worker(ch)                    // a green thread (Hemerodrome)
chan[int32] ch = chan()
ch.send(1)
int32 v = ch.recv()                 // waits for one

docs.title: Memory (NOVA)
docs.text:
Automatic, leak-free memory with no garbage collector; heap buffers are freed when their owner leaves scope. Today a transfer copies; (1.0) owning values move and .clone() copies (Memory Safety).

unsafe {
    ptr[int32] p = &x
    int32 val = *p
}

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text:
Annotation Purpose @cap(File\|Process\|Network\|Memory\|System) Declare a capability; callers must declare it too @pure / @io / @net Effects @tainted / @sanitizer / @sink Taint tracking @requires(cond) / @ensures(cond) Contracts (result is the return value); several are joined with && @sensitive Wipe the value's memory when it is freed @ignore_discard Callers may drop the return value @deprecated("msg") Callers get a warning @inline / @hot / @cold Inlining and code-placement hints @no_return The function never returns (return is an error; reaching the end aborts) @section("name") Place the function in a linker section @module_init / @module_exit A module's entry and exit points (.init.text / .exit.text) @repr("C") Lay a struct out exactly as C does (every field must have a C equivalent) @test A test function @cfg(...) Conditional compilation (target_arch, ptr_width, profile, feature); comes first

Annotations work the same on methods as on functions. An unknown or misplaced annotation is a compile error. (1.0): @packed, @aligned(N) and @opaque are rejected until C-compatible layouts land; annotations on struct fields and the call-site annotations on generic functions are not supported yet.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
import std.string.{split, trim}
import app.models.{User, load_user as load}
import app.models.Session              // one name
import app.util.*                      // every pub name
import geo.flat                        // qualified: flat.Point, flat.make()
import geo.round as r                  // r.Point
pub import self.core.{Point}           // re-export

Use import, not use. An explicit import beats *; two * imports offering one name make it ambiguous.

docs.title: Cross-compilation
docs.text:
Stenopos can build a binary for a different CPU than the one you are compiling on, in one command:

stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten

That produces an ARM64 Linux executable from, say, an x86-64 laptop. No separate steps, no hand-run llc.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The compiler emits target-neutral LLVM IR — it does not bake in a CPU or a memory layout. So the same compiled program can be lowered for any supported CPU; --target just tells the backend which one, and picks the matching cross C compiler to link with.

docs.title: Supported targets
docs.text:
--target Architecture Notes x86_64 64-bit Intel/AMD the host default aarch64 (alias arm64) 64-bit ARM phones, Raspberry Pi 4/5, Apple-class ppc64le 64-bit PowerPC (little-endian) riscv64 64-bit RISC-V hard-float armv7 (alias arm) 32-bit ARM (hard-float) Raspberry Pi 2/3, many embedded boards s390x 64-bit IBM Z (big-endian) i686 (alias x86) 32-bit Intel/AMD older / smaller x86 devices mipsel 32-bit MIPS (little-endian) routers, embedded mips64el 64-bit MIPS (little-endian) powerpc (alias ppc) 32-bit PowerPC (big-endian) routers, older Macs, embedded mips 32-bit MIPS (big-endian) routers, embedded

You can pass either the short name (aarch64) or the full triple (aarch64-linux-gnu).

All eleven run correct programs — every byte order and word size (32- and 64-bit, little- and big-endian) — checked on every change, so a target on this list will not silently break.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
--target shells out to the matching cross toolchain, so it must be installed:

Target Package (Debian/Ubuntu) aarch64 gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu ppc64le gcc-powerpc64le-linux-gnu riscv64 gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu armv7 gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf s390x gcc-s390x-linux-gnu i686 gcc-i686-linux-gnu mipsel gcc-mipsel-linux-gnu mips64el gcc-mips64el-linux-gnuabi64 powerpc gcc-powerpc-linux-gnu mips gcc-mips-linux-gnu

If the toolchain is missing, the compiler says exactly which package to install.

docs.title: Running the result
docs.text:
A cross-built binary runs on the real target device. To try it on your build machine, use an emulator:

stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app-arm64 main.sten
qemu-aarch64-static -L /usr/aarch64-linux-gnu ./app-arm64

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• --target is a build-only option — run, check, and emit-* ignore it (you cannot execute a foreign-CPU binary directly on the host).
  • Every cross build is Linux/ELF and keeps the same security hardening as a native build (PIE, full RELRO, non-executable stack, stack canaries).
  • The output is a normal ELF executable, indistinguishable in shape from a C program built with GCC for that CPU.

docs.title: Standard Library Reference
docs.text:
The standard library is written in Stenopos and ships with every Syntagma release (pinned by std.lock). Import what you use by name:

import std.string.{split, join, trim}
import std.math.{sqrt, gcd}

docs.title: Security notes for the network modules
docs.text:
What these modules do not protect you from yet, so you can decide what your program must do itself:

  • std.http server: slow clients and floods. Limits.timeout_ms bounds each read, not a whole request: a client that sends one byte just inside the timeout can hold a connection for a long time, and nothing caps how many connections are open at once. Behind the public internet, put the server behind a proxy that enforces both, or cap connections in your accept loop. Deadlines for the header block and the body, and a connection cap, are planned.
  • std.http output refuses a header name or value, a method or a path containing CR, LF or NUL, so a value from a request can't split a response or smuggle a second request.
  • std.tls speaks TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. verified() checks the certificate chain against the system's CAs and the host name; a setup step that fails stops the connection instead of continuing unverified. A closed connection's handle is dead: using it again fails rather than reaching another connection. There is no client-certificate or server support yet.
  • Taint. Data read from a socket, a request or a response is not marked tainted yet (see Taint tracking); check it before it reaches a shell, a path or a query.

docs.title: Built into every str
docs.text:
No import needed:

str s = "Hello, World!"
int64 n = s.len()
int32 b = s.byte_at(0)
str part = s.substring(0, 5)        // "Hello"
List[str] words = s.split(", ")
int64 at = s.index_of("World")      // 7, or -1
bool st = s.starts_with("Hello")
str t = "  hi  ".trim()
str one = str_from_byte(72)         // "H": a one-byte string, from a byte 0-255

A str is a sequence of bytes (UTF-8 for text, but any bytes are allowed). byte_at reads one byte, and str_from_byte makes a one-byte string from a value 0-255 (any other value stops the program, like an index out of bounds).

Everything else is in std.string:

import std.string.{contains, ends_with, to_upper, to_lower, from_code_point}

bool has = contains(s, "World")
str loud = to_upper(s)
str owl = from_code_point(0x1F989) ?? ""   // a Unicode character as UTF-8 (null if not one)

std.bytes.to_str turns a byte list back into a string (any bytes), the inverse of std.bytes.from_str.

Coming in 1.0

After import std.string, its functions are also callable as methods (s.contains("World")), and replace is added (ADR-0042).

The source and tests are in the std repository.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: The compiler, stenopos, is also the formatter, linter, doc generator, test runner and language server, so there are no extra tools to install. This page covers using them on single files. In a project, tagma fmt, tagma lint, tagma doc and tagma test run the same tools over all of its sources (see Projects with tagma).

docs.title: stenopos fmt
docs.text:
Format source to the canonical style: 4-space indentation by brace depth, trimmed trailing whitespace, collapsed blank runs, and a single trailing newline. Comments and string contents are preserved exactly.

stenopos fmt src/main.sten          # reformat in place
stenopos fmt --check src/*.sten     # report unformatted files, exit 1 (for CI)

Formatting is idempotent — running it on already-formatted code changes nothing.

docs.title: stenopos lint
docs.text:
Report style and correctness lints over the parsed source.

stenopos lint src/*.sten

The current checks cover naming conventions (snake_case for functions and parameters, PascalCase for types and enum variants) and flag empty function bodies. Exit code is 1 if any lints are found.

docs.title: stenopos doc
docs.text:
Generate a Markdown API reference for a module's public surface — its pub functions, structs, enums, traits, and type aliases, with full signatures and the prose from their /// doc comments.

stenopos doc src/vector.sten              # print to stdout
stenopos doc src/vector.sten -o vector.md # write a file

/// Computes the area of a circle given its radius.
pub func circle_area(float64 radius) -> float64 {
    return 3.14159 * radius * radius
}

renders the signature followed by "Computes the area of a circle given its radius."

docs.title: stenopos test
docs.text:
Discover the @test functions in a file, run them, and report pass/fail.

// math_test.sten
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 { return a + b }

@test
func test_add() -> void {
    if (add(2, 3) != 5) {
        fail("add(2, 3) should be 5")
    }
}

stenopos test math_test.sten
# running 1 test(s) from math_test.sten
# test test_add ...
# ok — 1 test(s) passed

A test signals failure by aborting (for example via fail); the runner reports a non-zero exit when any test fails.

docs.title: Seeing the generated code
docs.text:
stenopos emit-ir src/main.sten main.ll   # the LLVM IR the compiler produces

Coming

dump-tokens and dump-ast (the lexer's tokens and the parsed tree), and --verify-ir (a structural check of the generated IR) were tools of the earlier Rust compiler and haven't been rebuilt yet.

docs.title: stenopos explain
docs.text:
Every diagnostic is tagged with an error code — error[E0300]: .... Pass that code to stenopos explain for a long-form explanation of the whole class of problem, with guidance on how to fix it:

stenopos explain E0300

E0300 [type error]

The expected type does not match the actual type. Stenopos does not
perform implicit type conversions. Use `cast[T]()` for safe numeric
conversions or `.to_X()` methods for other conversions.

Codes are grouped by compiler phase: E01xx lexer, E02xx parser, E03xx type, E04xx memory/ownership, E05xx security. explain knows every standard code, so you can look one up straight from the error[...] tag in a build's output.

docs.title: stenopos lsp
docs.text:
The language server. Your editor starts it and talks to it over standard input and output using the Language Server Protocol.

  • Diagnostics come from the real type checker, run on the unsaved buffer, so they match a build exactly.
  • Hover, go to definition and completion use the compiler's own lexer, so they keep working while the file is mid-edit. They cover functions, methods, structs, classes, enums and traits, including the public names of modules the file imports.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
A small extension that starts stenopos lsp as its server:

import { ExtensionContext } from "vscode";
import { LanguageClient, TransportKind } from "vscode-languageclient/node";

export function activate(_ctx: ExtensionContext) {
  const serverOptions = { command: "stenopos", args: ["lsp"], transport: TransportKind.stdio };
  const clientOptions = { documentSelector: [{ scheme: "file", language: "stenopos" }] };
  new LanguageClient("stenopos", "Stenopos", serverOptions, clientOptions).start();
}

Register the stenopos language for .sten files in the extension's package.json (contributes.languages).

docs.title: Casting
docs.text:
cast[T](val)              // numeric conversion between integer and float types

Integer casts are exact or truncating as the widths require: widening a signed value sign-extends, widening an unsigned one zero-extends.

A widening that keeps every value happens without a cast (ADR-0044 D3): to a wider type of the same signedness, or from an unsigned type to a wider signed one. Where two integer types meet (an operator, an assignment, an argument, a return, a range's ends), the narrower widens; when neither holds every value of the other (int32 and uint32, int64 and uint64), it is an error that says so.

Coming in 1.0: unsafe_cast[T](val) (reinterpret, inside unsafe) and const_cast[T](val).

docs.title: Type aliases
docs.text:
type Meters = float64
type NodeId = uint64
type Index[V] = HashMap[str, V]
pub type Edges = List[NodeId]

An alias is transparent: it names an existing type and is interchangeable with it. It is declared at module level, private unless pub, imported by name, and may be generic. Self-reference, a wrong type-argument count and a non-type right side are rejected. See Variables and types.

docs.title: Effect System
docs.text:
Functions can declare what kind of effects they have, and the compiler holds them to it.

Annotation Means @pure No effects: no I/O, and it may call only other effect-bounded functions @io Performs I/O @net Uses the network 
@pure
func add(int32 a, int32 b) -> int32 {
    return a + b
}

@io
func show(int32 x) -> void {
    println("{x}")
}

A @pure function that prints, or that calls a function with no effect annotation (whose effects the compiler can't vouch for), is a compile error:

func helper() -> int32 {
    println("side effect")
    return 1
}

@pure
func p() -> int32 {
    return helper()     // error: `helper`'s effects are unverified
}

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A @pure function can be trusted completely: a math library marked @pure can't sneak in a file or network access. Pure functions are also trivial to test and safe to run in parallel.

For access to files, processes and the network, the stronger mechanism is capabilities: @cap(...) must be declared by every function on the call path.

docs.title: Security Overview
docs.text: Stenopos makes security properties part of the type system: the compiler rejects the program, rather than a runtime check catching it later.

docs.title: What the compiler enforces today
docs.text: Dimension What it does Example Memory safety (NOVA) Automatic, leak-free memory; no use-after-free or double free; bounds-checked indexing; checked integer overflow Memory Safety Null safety Only a T? can be null, and it must be checked before use Nullable types Taint tracking Untrusted data can't reach a @sink until a @sanitizer has cleaned it Taint Tracking Capabilities A function that touches files, processes or the network must declare @cap(...), and so must everything that calls it below Effects A @pure function can't do I/O or call anything whose effects are unknown Effect System Constant time A secret[T] value can't steer a branch or a division below Contracts @requires / @ensures are checked on every call Contracts Sensitive data @sensitive values are wiped when freed below

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
@cap(File)
func save(str text) -> void {
    discard write_file("/tmp/notes.txt", text)
}

@cap(File)
func main() -> int32 {
    save("hello")
    println(read_file("/tmp/notes.txt"))
    return 0
}

Remove @cap(File) from main and the program doesn't compile: main calls save, which needs the File capability. The resources are File, Process, Network, Memory and System. A dependency can't quietly start using the network, because its callers would have to grant it.

A function that needs several stacks one @cap per line or, from rc.7, lists them in one, separated by , or |; these mean the same:

@cap(File, Process)
@cap(File | Process)

@cap(File)
@cap(Process)

docs.title: Constant-time secrets
docs.text:
func main() -> int32 {
    secret[int32] key = secret(42)
    secret[int32] mixed = wrapping_add(key, secret(8))
    // if (key == 42) { ... }   // error: a secret value may not drive a branch
    // key + 8                  // error: a checked `+` would branch on its overflow
    return 0
}

Arithmetic on secrets is modular: use wrapping_add, wrapping_sub and wrapping_mul. A checked +, - or * branches on its overflow, and with a secret operand that branch would leak it. Dividing by a secret, indexing with one and shifting by one are errors for the same reason.

docs.title: Sensitive data
docs.text:
func main() -> int32 {
    @sensitive str password = "hunter2"
    println(password)
    return 0
}
// the buffer holding the password is wiped before it is freed

docs.title: Coming
docs.text:
• Constant-time code generation checked in the compiler's output (today the type rules hold; the generated machine code isn't checked yet).
  • Contracts proved at compile time, not only checked at run time.

docs.title: Taint Tracking
docs.text:
Taint tracking is a compile-time data-flow analysis that prevents injection attacks. Data from an untrusted source is tainted; anything computed from tainted data is tainted too; and a sink (a function that would be dangerous with untrusted input) refuses tainted data at compile time. A sanitizer returns clean data.

import std.string.{split, join}

@tainted
func read_param() -> str {          // a source: its result is tainted
    return "x'; DROP TABLE users"
}

@sanitizer
func sql_escape(str s) -> str {     // returns clean data: doubles every quote
    return join(split(s, "'"), "''")
}

@sink
func db_query(str sql) -> void {    // refuses tainted data
    println(sql)
}

func main() -> int32 {
    str name = read_param()
    // db_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")   // compile error
    str safe = sql_escape(name)
    db_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{safe}'")      // ok
    return 0
}

A variable can be marked as a source directly:

@tainted str input = arg(1)

Taint flows through assignments, string interpolation, concatenation and function calls.

docs.title: What it prevents
docs.text: SQL injection, command injection, HTML/XSS injection, path traversal, and any injection into a sink you define.

docs.title: Syntagma, tagma and stenopos
docs.text:
Syntagma: In progress Tagma: In progress

Three names, one toolchain, split the way Rust's is (cargo and rustc):

Name What it is You use it to Syntagma The toolchain as a whole, and its releases Install and update tagma The build tool, and (from rc.6) the package manager Work on a project: tagma new, build, run, test stenopos The compiler, also the language server Compile one file, or embed the compiler in other tools

Most of the time you only type tagma. The language is called Stenopos, like the platform, and its files are .sten.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
• Syntagma uses semantic versions (v1.0.0-rc.7, then v1.0.0, v1.1.0). tagma and stenopos always share that version, because they are built and tested together.
  • The language changes through editions, not version numbers. A project names its edition in Tagma.toml (edition = "2026", the first). One compiler accepts every edition it knows, and breaking changes only come with a new edition that a project opts into.
  • The standard library has its own versions. Each Syntagma release bundles one, pinned.

docs.title: Release contents
docs.text: Every release is signed in CI by the Stenopos release key and ships, for each of six architectures, a bundle with both commands, the runtime and the standard library. See Downloads.

docs.title: Packages and the registry
docs.text:
In progress

New in rc.6

Everything on this page ships in v1.0.0-rc.6. The registry's first package, stenopos/dotenv, follows shortly; until then the index is empty. Publishing is open to the Stenopos organization first.

docs.title: Using packages
docs.text:
$ tagma add stenopos/dotenv
       Added dotenv = stenopos/dotenv 1.0.0 (granted File)

tagma add picks the newest version (or the one you name, stenopos/dotenv@1.0.0), writes one line to Tagma.toml, and grants the package the capabilities that it and its dependencies use:

[dependencies]
dotenv = { package = "stenopos/dotenv", version = "1.0.0", allow = ["File"] }
  • Names are namespaced (stenopos/json), so nobody can squat a short name and you can see who owns a package. You import a package by the name on the left (import dotenv.{load}); tagma add --as env picks another.
  • version = "1.2" means "at least 1.2.0" in the 1.x line.
  • --allow File,Network (or --allow none) grants exactly that instead; if it is not enough for the package, add says which capability is missing and changes nothing.
  • After every edit tagma selects versions, fetches each package and checks its hash and grants. If anything fails, Tagma.toml, Tagma.lock and vendor/ are left exactly as they were.
  • The rest of Tagma.toml (comments, order) is kept as you wrote it.
$ tagma update            # every dependency, or: tagma update dotenv
     Updated dotenv: stenopos/dotenv 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0
$ tagma remove dotenv
     Removed dotenv (stenopos/dotenv)

tagma update moves each requirement to the newest version of its major version. A new major version is a different package: update mentions it, and tagma add stenopos/dotenv@2.0.0 moves to it. A new version that needs a capability you haven't granted is refused, naming it; raise the grant yourself if you trust it.

docs.title: Dependencies only get the powers you grant
docs.text:
Every package's capabilities (File, Network, Process, Memory, System) are computed when it is published. In Tagma.toml you grant each dependency the capabilities it may use:

[dependencies]
json = { package = "stenopos/json", version = "1.2", allow = [] }
files = { package = "stenopos/files", version = "1.0", allow = ["File"] }

If a new version of a JSON library suddenly wants Network, your build fails and names the package and the capability, instead of quietly giving it network access.

  • Grants pass down, never up. A package can give its own dependencies only what it was given: what a package may use is what every grant on every path to it allows (your grant, then each package's grant to its dependencies in its own Tagma.toml).
  • The compiler enforces it on the code. tagma checks the capabilities the registry recorded, and the compiler holds each package's source to the same limit: a function in it may declare only granted capabilities, so a package that misrecorded them still can't use more.
  • unsafe needs Memory; extern "C" and inline asm need System. Raw memory and foreign code could do anything, so granting System means trusting the package with everything.
  • Your own code and path dependencies are not limited.

docs.title: Predictable versions
docs.text:
tagma uses minimal version selection: for each package it takes the highest of the minimum versions anything asks for, and never a newer version that nobody asked for. Versions only move when you run tagma update or tagma add. Tagma.lock records exactly what was chosen.

Precisely: a requirement "1.2" selects the lowest published 1.x version that is at least 1.2.0, and that version's own requirements are followed in turn. For each package and major version, the build uses the highest version reached. Retracted versions are skipped, unless Tagma.lock already names one. tagma fetch (and add, update, or any build whose lock no longer matches Tagma.toml) writes the result to Tagma.lock:

version = 1

[[package]]
name = "stenopos/json"
version = "1.2.0"
repository = "https://github.com/Stenopos/json"
commit = "2222222222222222222222222222222222222222"
hash = "sha256:…"
caps = ["File"]
dependencies = ["stenopos/text 1.0.3"]

Each entry is a selected version with the commit and content hash its source must match, the capabilities its code uses, and the exact versions of its own dependencies (caps here records what each package uses; allow in Tagma.toml is what you grant). With --locked, a command fails instead of changing the lock, for CI.

docs.title: Integrity and trust
docs.text:
• The registry is a signed index (a git repository) recording each version's source commit and a hash of its files. It does not host code.
  • tagma checks that hash before compiling anything, and Tagma.lock records it, so every later build verifies against it.
  • The index carries a signed snapshot with a seven-day expiry, so an old or frozen copy of the index is detected.
  • Every version is signed by its publisher, and the registry's root key is kept offline.
  • The exact format is FORMAT.md in the registry repository, and tagma registry check checks a checkout against it, every signature included. The registry's CI runs it on every change.

docs.title: Fetching and checking
docs.text:
tagma build (and run, check, test) fetches what a project needs. If Tagma.lock still satisfies Tagma.toml, it is used as it is and the index isn't needed at all; otherwise tagma updates its copy of the index, selects versions and rewrites the lock first (tagma fetch does just that).

  • The index is a clone of the registry in ~/.cache/stenopos/registry. It is used only after every signature checks out against the root key built into tagma, and only with a snapshot that hasn't expired and isn't older than one already seen. Anything else is refused, and the previous copy is kept.
  • A package is fetched by its commit (from GitHub, then its mirror) into ~/.cache/stenopos/src/<namespace>/<name>/<version>, and used only if its files hash to the content hash in Tagma.lock. That is checked again on every build, so a file changed in the cache is noticed and fetched afresh.
  • --offline uses only the cache; --locked fails rather than change Tagma.lock (for CI).
  • STENOPOS_CACHE moves the cache. STENOPOS_REGISTRY_URL and STENOPOS_REGISTRY_ROOT (a file with the root public key) point tagma at another registry, such as a private one.

docs.title: Vendoring
docs.text:
$ tagma vendor
    Vendored 3 package(s) into vendor/ (commit it; builds use it and check every hash)

tagma vendor copies every locked package into vendor/<namespace>/<name>/<version>. A project with a vendor/ directory builds from it alone, with no network and no cache, and still checks each package against the content hash in Tagma.lock, so an edited vendored file is refused. add, remove and update keep vendor/ in step.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
A package is a library (src/lib.sten) with a namespace and a repository in Tagma.toml:

[package]
name = "dotenv"
namespace = "stenopos"
version = "1.0.0"
edition = "2026"
repository = "https://github.com/Stenopos/dotenv"

To release a version, raise version, commit, and tag the commit v<version>. The package's CI then runs tagma publish, which:

  1. takes the files of the tagged commit (uncommitted changes are never part of a version) and computes their content hash;
  2. tests the package, resolving its dependencies afresh;
  3. finds the capabilities its code uses (tagma caps);
  4. writes the version entry into a checkout of the registry, signs it with the publisher key, checks the whole checkout (tagma registry check), and commits it.

The registry's CI then re-derives the entry from the source (tagma registry verify: the files at the commit must hash to the recorded hash, and the manifest, dependencies and capabilities must match), re-signs the snapshot and publishes the index. tagma publish --dry-run --registry <checkout> shows the entry and the statement its signature covers without writing anything.

A published package depends only on registry packages (not paths), and a version can never be changed or removed, only retracted. CI acts only on tags signed by a Stenopos release signer, at the commit being built: write access to a package's repository is not enough to publish.

docs.title: Retracting a version
docs.text: A broken version is retracted by pushing a signed tag retract/<version> (git tag -s retract/1.2.0); CI runs tagma retract, which signs the retraction and commits it to the registry. A retracted version is never chosen for a new resolution (add, update), but a project whose Tagma.lock already names it keeps building.

docs.title: When a publisher key is compromised
docs.text: The registry's root key revokes it from a date. Every version that key signed on or after that date is revoked: unlike a retracted version, it is refused even where Tagma.lock names it. Once your copy of the index updates (tagma fetch, add, update), a build with a revoked version locked stops and names it; tagma fetch moves you to a version that isn't revoked. Because the registry only accepts entries dated the day they are published, a stolen key can't slip in a version dated before its revocation.

docs.title: What a package's code uses
docs.text:
$ tagma caps
caps = ["File"]
$ tagma check --allow none
error[E0400]: this function's `@cap(File)` needs the File capability, but this package is granted no capabilities

tagma check --allow <A,B> holds every file of the package to those capabilities, exactly as a project's grant would. tagma caps finds the smallest set the package compiles within: what its registry entry records.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does tagma add <ns/name>[@<version>] [--as <name>] [--allow <A,B>\|none] Depend on a package, granting what it uses tagma remove <name>... Stop depending on a package (by import name or package) tagma update [<name>...] Move to the newest version of each major version tagma fetch Update the index, select versions and fetch every package tagma vendor Copy the packages into vendor/ for builds with no network tagma caps The capabilities the package's own code uses tagma check --allow <A,B>\|none Check that the package's own code needs only those capabilities tagma publish --registry <checkout> --key <file> --publisher <name> [--tag <tag>] [--dry-run] Write and sign this commit's registry entry (CI runs it) tagma retract <version> --registry <checkout> --key <file> --publisher <name> Retract a published version (CI runs it on a retract/<version> tag) tagma registry check [<dir>] [--previous <dir>] Check a registry checkout: format, signatures, append-only history tagma registry verify [<dir>] [--previous <dir>] Re-derive each new entry from its source --locked Fail if Tagma.lock would change (for CI) --offline Use only the cache and vendor/; never the network --registry <checkout> Use a local registry checkout instead of the published index (checked the same way, except for the snapshot's expiry)

The standard library is not a registry package: it ships with Syntagma.

--feature NAME turns on @cfg(feature == "NAME") code.

docs.title: Tab completion
docs.text:
New in rc.8

Not in rc.7 or earlier releases.

Tab completes tagma and stenopos: commands and flags, --target and --allow values, .sten files where a source file goes, the error codes after stenopos explain, package names after tagma add (from the registry index tagma keeps; completion never uses the network), and your dependencies after tagma remove and tagma update.

The installer sets it up for bash, zsh and fish, under the install prefix's share/ directory, where each shell looks. To load it by hand (the same for stenopos):

source <(tagma completions bash)                               # in ~/.bashrc
source <(tagma completions zsh)                                # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit
tagma completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/tagma.fish

docs.title: Tagma.toml
docs.text:
[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2026"

[dependencies]
util = { path = "../util" }
  • name: letters, digits, - and _, starting with a letter.
  • version: the project's own semantic version.
  • edition: the language edition the project is written in.
  • namespace, repository: only for a package published to the registry: its namespace (stenopos) and its git repository's https:// URL.

A program's entry point is src/main.sten; a library's is src/lib.sten. check, test and doc work on both; build and run need a src/main.sten.

docs.title: Where tagma's messages go
docs.text:
tagma's progress lines (Compiling, Finished, Running, Added...) go to stderr, so a program's output under tagma run is the only thing on stdout: tagma run > out.txt holds just the program's. To send them elsewhere, or keep a log, add an [output] table to Tagma.toml:

[output]
status = "stdout"            # "stderr" (the default), "stdout", or "none"
log = "logs/build.log"       # also append everything tagma prints here

The log gets each run's command line ($ tagma build) and then everything written to stderr while it runs: tagma's messages, the compiler's diagnostics in full, a failing llc or cc. Its directory is made if needed. The program tagma run starts keeps its own output; for a log of what a program does, use std.logging.

For one run, the command line overrides the file: --status stdout|stderr|none, -q or --quiet (the same as --status none), and --log <file>. Errors always reach stderr, whatever status says, so a failure is never hidden.

docs.title: Build profiles
docs.text: tagma build makes a draft build: fast to compile and easy to debug. tagma build --release makes an optimized, stripped build that reads like a generic C binary. Every build is hardened: position-independent, full RELRO, a non-executable stack and stack protection.

docs.title: Wiping freed memory
docs.text:
@sensitive and secret[T] values are always zeroed when they are freed. A program can ask for every freed block to be zeroed, so that nothing it ever held stays readable in freed memory, whether or not it was marked:

[build]
wipe = "all"                 # or "secrets", the default

or stenopos build --wipe all for a single file. With all, every free zeroes the block first, and a buffer that grows (a string being built, a list being pushed to) is never left behind by realloc: a small one is copied and the old block wiped, and a large one (128 KiB or more, on Linux with glibc) lives in its own memory mapping and grows by moving its pages, with no copy at all. Large blocks are wiped only where their pages are resident, so wiping never adds memory. It costs nothing for code that computes; code that allocates and frees a lot runs somewhat slower (4% to 16% on the benchmarks; the default costs nothing), which is why it isn't the default. ADR-0040 has the measurements.

From rc.8. The runtime is built once per mode; when its install directory isn't writable (an install under /usr/local), the built runtime goes in ~/.cache/stenopos (rc.7 stopped with "Permission denied" there).

docs.title: Stack size
docs.text:
A program's main thread gets the system's stack, as a C program does: usually 8 MiB (ulimit -s shows it). A program that recurses deeply (a parser of deeply nested input, a recursive search) can ask for more:

[build]
stack = "256MiB"             # a number of bytes, or with KiB, MiB or GiB

or stenopos build --stack 256MiB for a single file. The program then raises its limit and starts itself again before main, once; a program that doesn't ask starts once and pays nothing. Running out of stack stops the program with stack overflow and this advice, not a bare "Segmentation fault". Programs that tagma or stenopos run start get the stack your shell gave them, never the toolchain's own (1 GiB), so what passes under tagma run behaves the same on its own.

On Linux a stack is virtual memory; the kernel decides which physical memory backs it, and only the pages a program touches use any.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text:
A project that runs on a board with no operating system (a boot loader, a device's firmware, an OS kernel) describes the board in Tagma.toml. tagma builds it freestanding, writes its linker script, and hands main the board's devices. The program runs on the board runtime, written in Stenopos, so strings, lists and println work as they do on a host. From rc.8 (ADR-0057, ADR-0058):

[target]
kind = "firmware"                 # no OS, no C library
arch = "riscv64"                  # riscv64, aarch64 or x86_64
console = { device = "uart0", put = "uart.put" }        # println, a failed check
halt = { device = "power", call = "sifive.power_off" }  # optional
float = "software"                # or "hardware": the FPU; optional

[memory]
ram = { origin = 0x8000_0000, size = "128MiB", kind = "code" }

[layout]
code  = "ram"                     # code and constants
data  = "ram"                     # statics
stack = { region = "ram", size = "64KiB" }
heap  = { region = "ram", size = "1MiB" }    # strings and lists; optional

[devices]
uart0 = { type = "uart.Ns16550", at = 0x1000_0000 }
power = { type = "sifive.SifiveTest", at = 0x10_0000 }
  • [memory] names the board's regions: each has an origin, a size (in bytes, or "64KiB", "128MiB", "1GiB") and a kind: code (executable RAM), data or rom (read-only, executable). Regions may not overlap.
  • [layout] says which region holds code, data and the stack, and the stack's size. With a single region it may be left out. heap takes the last size bytes of its region; the linker can place nothing there.
  • The linker script is generated from the two, into target/<profile>/link.ld: nobody writes one. A region that overflows fails the build, naming it, and every build reports each region's use:
   Compiling pathfinder v0.1.0 (release)
      Memory ram      64.5 KiB of 128 MiB (0.0%)
    Finished target/release/pathfinder
  • [devices] binds each device to an address: its type is a register block, named with the module it is declared in (uart.Ns16550 for src/uart.sten). A device may not sit inside a memory region or overlap another device.

The devices reach the program as a value. tagma writes target/board.sten on every build (a real file, to read; not to edit), with a Board that has one field per device, and main receives it:

import board.{Board}
import uart.{Ns16550, put}

func main(Board board) -> void {
    put(board.uart0, 65)          // board.uart0: the UART at 0x1000_0000
}

Using board.uart0 needs no unsafe: the address is Tagma.toml's, reviewed with the board, and each device is a constant address, so the board costs nothing at run time. Only tagma's generated file may declare a @board; a program that binds a device itself does so with registers_at inside unsafe. src/board.sten is refused, since board is the generated module's name.

tagma board shows it all, with where each part comes from:

Board: firmware for riscv64 (Tagma.toml:7)

Memory
  ram        0x80000000     128 MiB    code   Tagma.toml:12

Layout
  code    ram
  data    ram
  stack   ram, 64 KiB
  heap    ram, 1 MiB at 0x87f00000

Runtime
  console  uart.put on uart0   Tagma.toml:8
  halt     sifive.power_off on power   Tagma.toml:9

Devices
  uart0      uart.Ns16550         0x10000000     Tagma.toml:20
      used at src/main.sten:22: put(board.uart0, 65)

Every problem names its line:

Tagma.toml:20: device `uart0` at 0x80001000 is inside region `ram` (Tagma.toml:12)
error[E0300]: `board.uart1` doesn't exist: Tagma.toml declares uart0, power

The program brings its own start-up code (a @naked _start in section .text.start, which the linker script places first), as the pathfinder in stenopos-os shows for each architecture. @cfg(target_os == "none") selects code for a freestanding build.

docs.title: The board runtime
docs.text:
A freestanding program is compiled with the board runtime (stenopos_bare.sten, installed beside the C runtime): allocation over the heap, strings and number formatting, lists, println, and the checks' failures. It calls no C. It needs three things from the board, which tagma writes into target/board.sten from Tagma.toml:

  • The console: [target] console names the driver function that sends one byte (put = "uart.put", taking the device when device is given, or only the byte). println and a failed check's message go there. With no console they go nowhere.
  • Halting: [target] halt names the function that stops the board (powers it off, say). Without it the processor waits forever.
  • The heap: [layout] heap. Without it, the first allocation stops the board with out of memory.

A failed check prints the message a host program prints (integer overflow, stenopos: array index out of bounds: index 5, length 3), then halts; programs don't define the handlers. A throw is reported as uncaught: try isn't supported on a board yet. Maps and sorting come later; a program that uses them is refused by name when it's built.

docs.title: float64 on a board
docs.text:
By default a board build uses no floating-point or SIMD registers at all (ADR-0059): float64 is computed in software, by the board runtime's routines (the ones a C compiler's support library has, such as __adddf3, exact to IEEE 754), so float64 works as on a host, more slowly. With nothing in those registers, an interrupt handler's entry saves only the integer registers, and the start code needn't enable the FPU. This is how kernels are built.

float = "hardware" in [target] uses the FPU instead: faster arithmetic, and every interrupt entry saves the FP/SIMD state as well. The start code must enable the FPU before any float64 runs: mstatus.FS on RISC-V, CPACR_EL1.FPEN on ARM64, CR4.OSFXSR on x86-64. println and "{x}" print a float64 as a host program does (C's %g) either way, and tagma board shows which a board uses.

On ARM64 the compiler never emits an unaligned access (memory is device memory until the program turns the MMU on).

Interrupt handlers (@interrupt, interrupt_entry), statics and memory_fence() are in Memory safety.

Still to come (ADR-0057): placing functions and statics in a region (@place), proven stack bounds, and boards as packages.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Today a dependency is a local path to another project. Its src/ directory becomes an import root:

util/src/lib.sten        module util ... pub func greet(str who) -> str
hello/src/main.sten      import util.{greet}

Registry packages are added with tagma add; see Packages and the registry.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
// tests/math.sten
@test
func adds() -> void {
    if (1 + 1 != 2) {
        fail("math is broken")
    }
}

tagma test

A test in tests/ imports the project's own modules (import dotenv.{parse} for a library whose src/lib.sten is module dotenv). A test function that needs a capability declares it, like any function:

@cap(File)
@test
func reads_config() -> void {
    if (read_file("Tagma.toml") == "") {
        fail("no manifest")
    }
}

docs.title: Single files
docs.text: stenopos keeps its single-file commands (stenopos run file.sten, build, check, fmt, lint, doc, test). Inside a project, it points you to tagma instead.

docs.title: Stenopos OS
docs.text:
Designed

Stenopos OS is a memory-safe, capability-based operating system written in Stenopos. It is designed to be the hardest place for an attack to get through, while still running the world's software: native .pano apps, Debian packages through apt-get, and Windows .exe programs, on hardware from Raspberry Pis to servers and phones.

Designed, not yet built

The design is complete and recorded in architecture decision records. Building starts with the foundations (see the roadmap). These pages explain the design.

docs.title: The design in brief
docs.text:
• Written by us, in Stenopos. The boot loader, the nucleus, the drivers, the services, the shell, the desktop, its toolkit and the web engine are all written for this OS in one memory-safe language. Nothing in the system image is a port of someone else's C or C++. The few things that cannot be ours (hardware firmware, standard data such as Unicode tables and root certificates, fonts) are signed, converted to our own checked formats at build time, and treated as untrusted input. Software you install yourself (a Linux or Windows program, another browser) runs confined, outside the system.

  • A small verified core. The nucleus (L0) is the only code with full control of the hardware, and it is formally verified.

  • Everything else in compartments. Drivers, filesystems, the network stack and the syscall layer each run in their own hardware-isolated compartment. A bug in one cannot reach the others.
  • No root. All authority is capabilities: specific, delegable and revocable. Administration is a scoped grant you confirm on a trusted path.
  • An immutable system. The system image is verified at boot, updated atomically, and rolled back automatically if an update fails.
  • Apps get what they declare. Each app lists the capabilities it needs, and nothing else is reachable.
  • Honest about hardware. The OS reports the security tier the hardware allows and never weakens protection silently.
