docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.7: Stenopos Now Compiles Itself
docs.text:
This is the release we have been building toward since alpha.1: Stenopos is self-hosting. There is now a Stenopos compiler written in Stenopos, it compiles its own source code, and the compiler it produces is byte-for-byte identical to the one that built it. That loop — a compiler building itself, and getting the same answer — is the oldest proof of seriousness a language can offer. C did it in 1973. Now Stenopos has done it too.

And it is fast: the self-hosted compiler builds a 7,000-line benchmark about twice as fast as gcc -O0 builds the same program in C.

docs.title: What self-hosting means (and why you should care)
docs.text:
Think of a language as a set of tools. The question every new language must answer is: are the tools good enough to build real things? The most honest test is to build the hardest thing the language's authors know how to build — the language's own compiler — using nothing but the language itself.

That is what this release does. The pipeline works like this:

  1. A frozen "seed" compiler (the original Rust implementation) builds stage1 — the Stenopos compiler written in Stenopos.
  2. stage1 compiles its own source code, producing stage2.
  3. stage2 compiles the same source again, producing stage3.
  4. We check that stage2 and stage3 are byte-identical.

If anything in the compiler were wrong — a mis-parsed expression, a miscompiled loop, a dropped declaration — the copies would drift apart. They don't. The fixpoint holds, and our CI re-proves it on every single commit, along with 13 test programs (including the compiler's own unit-test suites and a set of programs that must be rejected with the right error messages) compiled and run by the self-built compiler.

The Rust implementation is now the bootstrap seed: it is kept only so a fresh machine can build stage1. New compiler work happens in Stenopos.

docs.title: Faster than gcc
docs.text:
Along the way the self-compile went from 103 seconds to about 1 second. Two things were responsible, and both are lessons in how much allocation behavior matters:

  • The code generator built its output with body = body + chunk — which re-copies the entire growing buffer on every append. Tens of thousands of appends made that O(n²): 70 of the 103 seconds were spent copying the same bytes over and over. The fix is the new List[str].join(): collect chunks in a list (each push is cheap) and stitch them together once at the end, in a single pass.
  • The backend invoked LLVM at its default optimization level, produced assembly text, and recompiled the C runtime from source on every link. Now it goes straight to an object file with fast instruction selection and links against a cached runtime object.

The result, measured on identical 500-function programs (~7,000 lines each) written in C and in Stenopos, end-to-end from source to runnable binary:

Compiler Time gcc -O0 (C) 0.81 s Stenopos, self-hosted 0.42 s Stenopos (Rust seed) 0.58 s

All three binaries print the same answer. (Honest footnote: both compilers are at the no-optimization level, and Stenopos's self-hosted compiler does less analysis than gcc. But "compiles its own language about 2× faster than gcc compiles C" is a real number, and it is the floor, not the ceiling.)

docs.title: The language grew, because writing a compiler demands it
docs.text:
Self-hosting is a forcing function: every gap in a language shows up the moment you try to write real code in it. This release ships everything the compiler-in-Stenopos needed, so you get it too:

for over lists — the third form of Stenopos's one loop now works on List[T]:

List[str] words = list_new()
words.push("sten")
words.push("opos")
for (w in words) {
    println(w)
}
for (i, w in words) {
    println("{i}: {w}")
}

The binding is a fresh copy of each element, and anything heap-owning is freed automatically at the end of every iteration — even on break or continue. Valgrind-clean, like every memory feature in Stenopos.

List[str].join() — flatten a list of strings in one pass. If you ever find yourself writing s = s + chunk in a loop, use a list and join() instead; your program stops being accidentally quadratic:

List[str] parts = list_new()
parts.push("Hello, ")
parts.push("Stenopos")
parts.push("!")
str greeting = parts.join()

fail(msg) — print to stderr and exit(1). The abort primitive every command-line tool needs for fatal errors; the self-hosted compiler uses it for its own diagnostics:

if (value < 0) {
    fail("value must be non-negative, got {value}")
}

docs.title: The compiler is also a program you can read
docs.text:
One more thing worth saying plainly. The Stenopos-in-Stenopos compiler — a lexer, a recursive-descent parser, an LLVM IR code generator, and a driver — is about 5,000 lines of ordinary Stenopos: structs with methods, enums with payloads, match, lists, strings. It manages all of its memory through the language's automatic ownership (NOVA); the generated compiler runs leak-clean under Valgrind. When it finds a mistake in your program it says things like:

stenopos: line 12: function 'secret' is private to module 'lib.a' - mark it pub
stenopos: line 3: unknown name 'typo'

A compiler is not a magic artifact. It is a program, and now it is a Stenopos program.

docs.title: Everything else in alpha.7
docs.text:
The full changelog is long — this is the biggest release since alpha.1 — but highlights beyond the headline:

  • stenopos stat: line counts by language and kind across a source tree, including the self-hosting percentage.
  • Compound assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=) and for loops in the self-hosted subset, string interpolation, float64 (including List[float64]), and module visibility with line-numbered diagnostics.
  • The automated bootstrap check (scripts/bootstrap.sh) runs in CI on every commit: fixpoint + 13 programs through the self-built compiler in ~8 s.

docs.title: Getting alpha.7
docs.text:
Grab a binary from the GitHub release (x86_64 and aarch64 Linux, with SHA256SUMS), or use the installer. Examples live in the examples repository.

What's next: growing the self-hosted compiler toward the full language — finer-grained visibility, richer collections — and the standard library, written in Stenopos, of course.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.8: A Standard Library, Real Modules, and a Growing Self-Hosted Compiler
docs.text: Yesterday Stenopos learned to compile itself. Today's release is about what a language does the morning after: it gets a standard library, its modules grow real walls, and the self-hosted compiler keeps absorbing the language it is written in — hash maps, floating point, string interpolation, proper error messages with line numbers.

docs.title: The standard library, written in Stenopos
docs.text:
There is now a std repository with four implemented, tested modules — string, math, collections, and io — all pure Stenopos. Even sqrt is Newton's method in Stenopos, no C library in sight:

import std.string.{trim, to_upper, split}
import std.math.{gcd, sqrt}

func main() -> void {
    println(to_upper(trim("  stenopos  ")))   // STENOPOS
    List[str] parts = split("a,b,c", ",")    // 3 parts
    println("gcd: {gcd(48, 36)}")            // 12
    println("sqrt2: {sqrt(2.0)}")            // 1.41421
}

And the compiler knows how to find it: point STENOPOS_STD at the std tree (or ship a std/ directory next to the binary) and import std.* resolves like any local module. Everything still compiles from source as one program — no binary library format, no linker surprises.

docs.title: Modules with real walls
docs.text:
Until now, pub was a promise Stenopos didn't check. The self-hosted compiler now enforces the whole story, with line-numbered errors:

stenopos: line 8:  struct 'Hidden' is private to module 'lib.a' - mark it pub
stenopos: line 7:  struct 'Vis' is not imported by module 'app.b' - add it to an import line
stenopos: line 12: method 'peek' of struct 'Box' is private to module 'lib.a' - mark it pub
stenopos: line 12: field 'v' of struct 'Box' is private to module 'lib.a' - mark it pub

Functions, structs, enums, methods, and — new in this release — individual fields are private by default; crossing a module boundary requires pub and an import. And modules are now true namespaces: two modules may each have their own private helper() without colliding — the compiler mangles emitted names per module and resolves calls to your own module first, then to what you imported.

docs.title: The subset closes in on the language
docs.text:
The compiler-written-in-Stenopos gained, since alpha.7:

  • HashMap[str, V] — including passing maps to functions (borrowed, so the callee's inserts persist), returning them (an owned copy), storing them in struct fields, and m2 = m1 deep copies. Valgrind-clean, like everything else.
  • for loops and compound assignment (+= and friends) — pure parse-time sugar; the compiler's own source now uses them.
  • float64, string interpolation, and hard diagnostics — an unknown name, a private field, a duplicate function: each is a clear error with a line number instead of a silent mis-parse.

Every commit, CI rebuilds the compiler with itself and checks the result is byte-identical, then runs 19 programs through the self-built compiler — including its own three unit-test suites and eight programs that must be rejected with exactly the right error message.

docs.title: Getting alpha.8
docs.text:
Binaries for x86_64 and aarch64 Linux are on the GitHub release, with SHA256SUMS. The std library lives in the std repository; set STENOPOS_STD to its checkout to use import std.* today.

Next: per-module types, richer std (the kernel bindings are waiting on freestanding codegen), and the long road of teaching the self-hosted compiler the rest of its own language.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.9: Exceptions, Real Interpolation, and a Bigger Standard Library
docs.text: Alpha.9 fills in three things you reach for constantly: exception handling in the self-hosted compiler, string interpolation that works everywhere (not just inside println), and two more standard-library modules. Two of the changes started as bug hunts — and the bugs they turned up were the good kind, the kind that were quietly wrong for a while.

docs.title: try / catch / throw
docs.text:
The compiler-written-in-Stenopos can now handle exceptions:

func risky(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n < 0) {
        throw("negative input")
    }
    return n * 2
}

func classify(int32 n) -> str {
    str out = "?"
    try {
        int32 v = risky(n)
        out = "ok:{v}"
    } catch (str e) {
        out = "err:{e}"
    }
    return out
}

throw long-jumps to the innermost try, and the catch binds the thrown message to its variable. Nested try/catch and re-throwing both work. It is built on setjmp/longjmp, the same mechanism a C program would use — which comes with the same caveat: don't return straight out of a try block (assign a result and return after), and heap allocated on the throw path may leak. Stenopos's own compiler reports errors by returning diagnostics, not by throwing, so those limits are fine in practice; the feature exists so the language's try/catch can itself be self-hosted.

docs.title: Interpolation that works as a value
docs.text:
String interpolation has been in Stenopos since early on — but only ever inside println. This release found and fixed the gap: interpolating into a value you keep.

str name = "stenopos"
str s = "hi {name}"                       // now works
str g = greeting(name, 3)                 // returned from a function
println(greeting("world", 0).len())       // passed along and measured

The old code path for "interpolation not in a println" was a stub that returned only the first literal chunk — so str s = "hi {name}" printed hi and, worse, later crashed when the automatic memory manager tried to free what turned out to be a pointer into static memory. It now formats into a real owned string. If you ever assigned an interpolated string to a variable and got a truncated result, this is your fix.

docs.title: A bigger standard library
docs.text:
Two new modules land in the std repository:

  • std.testing — a small unit-test framework (expect, expect_eq_int, expect_eq_str, report), the same shape the compiler's own tests use. It tests itself.
  • std.os — named wrappers over the process and argument built-ins: run / run_ok to shell out, and argc / arg_at / args / has_flag to read the command line.
import std.testing.{expect_eq_int, report}
import std.os.{run, has_flag}

func main() -> int32 {
    int32 fails = 0
    fails += expect_eq_int(run("true"), 0, "true exits 0")
    return report(fails)
}

That brings std to six tested modules — string, math, collections, io, testing, os — all pure Stenopos, and all resolvable with import std.* once you point STENOPOS_STD at the checkout.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text: Both feature bugs surfaced while writing tests for the new work, and both were memory-safety issues the compiler's own Valgrind-clean discipline caught immediately: a thrown string literal was being freed as if it were owned, and the interpolation stub was freeing static memory. Fixing them made the whole thing tighter. As always, every commit rebuilds the compiler with itself, checks the result is byte-identical, and runs a growing corpus — now 20 programs — through the self-built compiler.

docs.title: Getting alpha.9
docs.text:
Binaries for x86_64 and aarch64 Linux are on the GitHub release, with SHA256SUMS. The standard library is in the std repository.

Next: growing the standard library further, and continuing to teach the self-hosted compiler the rest of its own language.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-alpha.10: Generic Lists, and Exceptions That Clean Up After Themselves
docs.text: Alpha.10 is a "sand off the rough edges" release. Two edges in particular: you can now write generic functions over List[T], and try/catch/finally finally behaves the way you expect on every path — including the awkward ones, like returning straight out of a try.

docs.title: Generics that understand lists
docs.text:
Stenopos has had generic functions for a while — func identity[T](T x) -> T and friends. But the moment you tried to be generic over a list of something, the compiler stopped you:

func first[T](List[T] xs) -> T {   // "List[<generic>] is not supported yet"
    return xs.get(0)
}

That gap is closed. The type parameter is now matched structurally: when you call first(nums) with a List[int32], the compiler looks inside the list type, binds T to int32, and stamps out a specialized copy of the function just for that case. Call it again with a List[str] and you get a second copy. Each copy is a concrete function, so strings are still cloned and freed exactly right — the whole thing is leak-free under valgrind.

func doubled[T](List[T] xs) -> List[T] {
    List[T] out = list_new()
    for (x in xs) { out.push(x) }
    for (x in xs) { out.push(x) }
    return out
}

The same matching works for ptr[T], T?, and other wrappers — anywhere the type parameter is nested one layer deep instead of sitting bare.

docs.title: A new standard-library module: std.list
docs.text:
With that in place, the standard library grows a genuinely generic list module. Where std.collections has to spell out the element type (sum_i32, sum_f64 — you can't add up strings), std.list doesn't care what's inside:

import std.list.{first, last, contains, index_of, reverse, take}

bool has = contains(names, "stenopos")   // works for List[str]
int32 i  = index_of(nums, 42)           // ...and List[int32]
List[str] r = reverse(names)

It ships with first/last, contains/index_of/count, and copy/concat/fill/reverse/take/drop — the small, everyday operations you'd otherwise rewrite in every project.

docs.title: finally, done properly
docs.text:
try/catch/finally looks simple, but the corner cases are where languages quietly cheat. This release fixes three of them.

Returning out of a try now works. Before, you had to stash your answer in a variable and return after the block. Now you can just return — and the finally still runs, and the exception machinery is cleaned up so a later throw still lands where it should:

func read_config(bool ok) -> int32 {
    try {
        if (ok) { return 200 }
        throw("missing config")
    } catch (Error e) {
        return 500
    } finally {
        println("closed config handle")   // runs on BOTH returns
    }
}

A try/finally with no catch no longer eats the exception. Previously, a block that only had a finally would run its cleanup and then carry on as if nothing had gone wrong — swallowing the error. Now it runs the finally and re-raises, so the exception travels on to the next handler out. That's the whole point of a bare try/finally: guarantee the cleanup, but don't pretend the failure didn't happen.

And the leaks are gone. A string (or list, or map) built inside a try body used to leak if a throw jumped past it, because the jump skips the normal end-of-scope cleanup. Those locals are now freed at the throw site, before the jump. The droppability analysis was also simply not looking inside try blocks at all, so any heap local declared in one leaked on every path — that's fixed too, and the catch variable's own copy is now freed when the catch block ends. The common paths are clean under valgrind.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
None of this disturbs the self-hosting story: the Rust seed still compiles the Stenopos compiler, which still compiles itself to a byte-identical fixpoint, and the full bootstrap — 24 programs through the self-built compiler — stays green.

As always: try/catch/finally is Stenopos's only error model (no ? operator), and memory is managed for you by NOVA. Alpha.10 just makes both of those a little more honest.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.1: Out of Alpha
docs.text: Stenopos is leaving alpha. v1.0.0-beta.1 is the first beta — the point where the language has all three of the things we said had to be true before we'd call it one: a real module system, real generics, and a real error model, on top of a compiler that already compiles itself.

docs.title: What "beta" means here
docs.text:
We set the bar for leaving alpha a long time ago, and it was deliberately concrete — no moving goalposts:

  • Modules — multi-file builds, per-module namespaces. ✓
  • Generics — generic functions, generic structs, generic List[T], and now traits. ✓
  • Error model — try / catch / finally, with the corner cases (return out of a try, re-raising from a bare try/finally) actually correct. ✓
  • Self-hosting — the trigger to leave alpha. The Stenopos compiler compiles itself to a byte-identical fixpoint, and has since alpha.7. ✓

The one piece still missing on that list was traits. This release lands them, so here we are.

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
A trait is a shared interface: a set of methods a type promises to provide. You declare one, implement it for your types, and then write code against the trait instead of against any one type.

trait Describable {
    func name() -> str
    func describe() -> str {     // a default — impls may inherit this
        return "a thing"
    }
}

impl Describable for Dog {
    func name() -> str { return "Dog" }
    func describe() -> str { return "a dog that says {this.sound}" }
}

impl Describable for Cat {
    func name() -> str { return "Cat" }   // inherits the default describe()
}

Trait bounds on a generic parameter let one function work over every type that implements the trait:

func announce[T: Describable](T x) -> void {
    println("here is a {x.name()}")
}

Two things worth saying about how this works under the hood, because they're choices, not accidents:

  • Dispatch is static. Each call to announce is monomorphized — the compiler stamps out a specialized copy for each concrete type it's called with, and the method call goes straight to that type's implementation. No vtable, no pointer chase, no runtime cost. It's the zero-overhead path.
  • Dispatch is by name, not by shape. If two different structs happen to have the same field layout, generic dispatch still calls the right one. (That sounds obvious; it's the kind of thing a structural backend gets wrong if you don't take care, so we took care — and there's a regression test for exactly that case.)

Default methods are inherited when an impl doesn't override them, an impl that forgets a required method is a compile error, and inherent impl blocks (no trait) let you hang plain methods on a type.

docs.title: Also in this release
docs.text: • A miscompile fix: calling a method directly on a call that returns a List or HashMap — make_list().len() — used to silently read an empty container and return 0. It now works (and no longer leaks the temporary).

docs.title: What beta doesn't mean
docs.text: Beta means the core language is here and coherent, not that it's finished. The road to 1.0 still runs through concurrency (green threads), the full security type system, cross-compilation, and a package manager. But the shape of the language you'd write real programs in is now settled — and it compiles itself to prove it.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.2: The Trait System, Finished — and Release Signing Lands
docs.text: Beta.1 landed traits. Beta.2 finishes them — impls on primitives, generic impls, dynamic dispatch, and associated types — and lands GPG-signed releases, starting with the next build, so you can verify what you download.

docs.title: Signed releases
docs.text:
Release signing is landing. Starting with the next release, the build pipeline GPG-signs the checksum file for every tag, shipping a SHA256SUMS.asc signature and the public key (stenopos-signing-key.asc) right alongside the binaries. Once a release carries a SHA256SUMS.asc, you can verify a download end to end without hunting anything down:

# Download the binary, SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.asc, and stenopos-signing-key.asc
# from the release, then:
gpg --import stenopos-signing-key.asc
gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS   # authentic checksums
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS                  # binaries match the checksums

A Good signature from "StenoposBuild" means the bytes you have are the bytes we built.

docs.title: The trait system is complete
docs.text:
Beta.1 shipped the core: trait declarations, impls, default methods, and static (monomorphized) dispatch with trait bounds on generics. Beta.2 fills in the four remaining pieces.

Impls on primitives. You can implement a trait for int32, bool, str, and the rest — the receiver this is the value itself:

impl Describable for int32 {
    func describe() -> str { return "the int {this}" }
}

Generic impls. Implement a trait for a generic struct across every element type at once; the methods are monomorphized alongside the struct:

impl[T] Show for Box[T] {
    func show() -> str { return "Box holding {this.value}" }
}

Dynamic dispatch — dyn Trait. When you need one value that could be any implementer, chosen at runtime, use a trait object:

dyn Speak a = Dog { sound: "grr" }
dyn Speak b = Robot { id: 7 }
println(a.say())   // dispatched through a vtable
println(b.say())

A dyn Trait is a fat pointer { data, vtable } — the C++ virtual-call model, but non-intrusive: a plain Dog stays plain data and only carries a vtable when used as dyn. The trait object owns its boxed value and frees it (and any owned fields) automatically.

Associated types. A trait can declare a type each impl fills in — resolved at compile time, zero runtime cost, just like a C++ member typedef:

trait Container {
    type Item
    func first() -> Item
}
impl Container for IntBox {
    type Item = int32
    func first() -> int32 { return this.value }
}

And where the two features meet, Stenopos enforces object safety the same way C++ and Rust do: a trait with associated types can't be used as dyn (the type would be erased) — a clean compile error, never a silent miscompile.

docs.title: Design choices, on the record
docs.text:
Two calls worth stating plainly, both aimed at staying close to C/C++:

  • Static by default, dynamic on request. Ordinary trait calls cost nothing extra — they compile to a direct call. You only pay for a vtable when you write dyn.
  • dyn is a vtable, not a tagged union. It's the mechanism C++ programmers already know (and the Linux kernel's struct file_operations is a hand-rolled version of it), and unlike a closed tagged union it doesn't need to know every implementer up front.

The full write-up is in docs/TRAITS.md.

As always: memory is managed for you (every trait object and boxed value is freed automatically, valgrind-clean), the compiler still compiles itself, and release signing is landing.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.3: Signed, for Real
docs.text: Beta.2 promised signed releases. Beta.3 delivers them — this is the first Stenopos release you can cryptographically verify.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
The build pipeline now GPG-signs every tagged release. Each release carries two new files next to the binaries: a SHA256SUMS.asc detached signature and the public key, stenopos-signing-key.asc. The signing key lives in the CI secret store and never touches the source tree.

That is the whole release, and it is an honest one. Beta.2 announced signing but shipped just before the pipeline was finished, so it went out unsigned — a footnote we added to that post. Beta.3 is the fix: signing is on, and it stays on for every release from here.

docs.title: Verify a download
docs.text:
Grab the binary, SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.asc, and stenopos-signing-key.asc from the release, then:

gpg --import stenopos-signing-key.asc
gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS   # the checksums are authentic
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS                  # the binaries match the checksums

A Good signature from "StenoposBuild" means the bytes you downloaded are the exact bytes we built. (gpg may also print a note that the key is not "trusted" — that only means you have not personally vouched for it yet. The signature is still valid.)

docs.title: Why bother this early?
docs.text: Because trust is easier to build than to retrofit. A verifiable download chain is the kind of thing you want in place before anyone runs Stenopos on something that matters — not bolted on afterward. Everything else from beta.2 still holds: the trait system is complete, memory is managed for you, and the compiler still compiles itself.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.4: Null Safety, the Kotlin Way
docs.text: The billion-dollar mistake, refused at compile time. Beta.4 adds nullable types — a value that might be null is a different type, and the compiler makes you check before you use it.

docs.title: A value, or nothing
docs.text:
A T? holds either a T or null:

int32? maybe = null
str?   name  = "Stenopos"

You cannot use a T? as a T by accident. This is a compile error, not a crash later:

int32? x = 5
int32  y = x        // error: cannot use int32? as int32 — check for null first

docs.title: The compiler narrows for you
docs.text:
Once you rule out null, the compiler knows the value is there, and lets you use it as the plain type — no ceremony:

func classify(int32? n) -> str {
    if (n == null) {
        return "none"
    }
    // from here on, `n` is a plain int32
    if (n > 0) {
        return "positive: {n}"
    }
    return "non-positive: {n}"
}

That works inside an if (n != null) { … } block too, and after an early return guard like the one above.

docs.title: Two operators for the common cases
docs.text:
When you just want a fallback, use ??:

int32? missing = null
println("{missing ?? 0}")     // 0

When you are certain it is not null and want to say so, use !! (it panics at runtime if you are wrong):

int32? forced = 7
println("{forced!!}")          // 7

docs.title: And it stays memory-safe
docs.text: A nullable string owns its text like any other string — you never free anything, and there are no leaks. We check every example under Valgrind, and the nullable ones are clean across assignment, reassignment, loops, narrowing, ??, and !!.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: One piece of the null story is still on the way: the safe-access operator ?. (node?.value, name?.len()). It reports a clear "not yet" for now, and it's the very next thing we're building. Everything else about null safety is here in beta.4 — and, as always, the release is GPG-signed and the compiler still compiles itself.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.5: Safe Access, and Null Safety Complete
docs.text: Beta.4 made a value that might be null a different type. Beta.5 adds the last operator — ?. — and closes the loop: null safety is now complete.

docs.title: Reach in safely
docs.text:
The safe-access operator ?. lets you read a field or call a method on a nullable value without a manual check. If the value is there, you get the result; if it is null, the whole expression is null:

str? name = "Stenopos"
int64 length = name?.len() ?? 0     // 7

It works on struct fields and struct methods too, and — like everything about a nullable — the result is itself nullable, so you pair it with ?? to land on a plain value:

Point? here = Point { x: 3, y: 4 }
Point? nowhere = null
println("{(here?.manhattan()) ?? 0}")     // 7
println("{(nowhere?.x) ?? 0}")            // 0

docs.title: Nullable structs, all the way through
docs.text:
Your own types can be nullable now — Point? p parses and works end to end: declaration, == null, and flow narrowing that reaches into the value. After a null check, you can read fields and call methods on it directly:

func describe(Point? p) -> str {
    if (p == null) {
        return "nowhere"
    }
    // `p` is a plain Point here — field access and methods just work
    return "at {p.x}, {p.y} (dist {p.manhattan()})"
}

And if that struct owns a string, it is freed for you when the nullable goes out of scope — every nullable path is Valgrind-clean.

docs.title: The whole null story, in one place
docs.text: That completes the set: T?, null, ==/!= null with narrowing, ??, !!, and now ?.. examples/nullable.sten shows all of it in one program. As always, the release is GPG-signed and the compiler still compiles itself.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.6: Safer by Default, and a Toolbox to Match
docs.text: Beta.5 finished null safety. Beta.6 hardens the everyday paths — arithmetic, assumptions, cleanup, and module boundaries — and hands you the tools every project reaches for on day one.

docs.title: Integer overflow traps instead of wrapping
docs.text:
int32 x = 2147483647; x + 1 used to silently become -2147483648. That is the quiet start of a whole class of security bugs — a wrapped size calculation that allocates a buffer that is too small. In beta.6 it stops the program instead:

integer overflow: add of two int32 values

Every +, -, and * on an integer is checked, signed and unsigned, in expressions and compound assignments. The in-range path stays cheap (an add plus a jump-on-overflow). When you want modular arithmetic — hashes, checksums, ring buffers — say so:

uint32 hash = wrapping_mul(hash, 16777619)

docs.title: Contracts: state your assumptions, and hold them
docs.text:
@requires and @ensures attach a precondition and a postcondition to a function. Both are checked at run time; inside @ensures, result is the returned value. A broken assumption halts at the boundary that stated it.

@requires(n >= 0)
@ensures(result >= 1)
func factorial(int32 n) -> int32 {
    if (n <= 1) { return 1 }
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
}

docs.title: defer, block-scoped
docs.text:
defer schedules cleanup that runs when its block exits — on the happy path, an early return, a break/continue, or a throw — last-in-first-out, and before the block's locals are freed. It is block-scoped, so a defer in a loop body fires once per iteration:

for (i in 0..2) {
    defer println("close {i}")
    println("open {i}")
}
// open 0 / close 0 / open 1 / close 1 / open 2 / close 2

docs.title: Copies are deep copies — no aliasing surprises
docs.text: Copying a struct, list, or map now duplicates the heap it owns, so the copy is fully independent of the original. Mutating one never touches the other, and each is freed exactly once. (This also closed a double-free that could happen when two names shared one buffer.)

docs.title: Module boundaries are real
docs.text: A declaration is private to its module unless you mark it pub. Reaching for a private name from another module is a compile error — your public surface is exactly what you chose to expose, and everything else stays yours to change.

docs.title: One binary, four tools
docs.text:
The toolchain now formats, lints, documents, and tests:

stenopos fmt --check src/*.sten   # canonical formatting (CI-friendly)
stenopos lint src/*.sten          # naming + style checks
stenopos doc src/vector.sten      # Markdown API reference from /// comments
stenopos test math_test.sten      # run the file's @test functions

stenopos fmt is idempotent and preserves your comments; stenopos doc pulls the prose from /// comments straight into the reference.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

As always, every release is checksummed, signed, and verified against the public example suite before it ships.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.7: We Pointed the Tools at Ourselves
docs.text: beta.6 shipped stenopos fmt, lint, doc, and test. The natural next step was to run them across our own Stenopos code — the examples and the standard library — and wire that into CI so those repositories stay clean on every change. Doing that found a real bug in the formatter. beta.7 fixes it.

docs.title: The bug: a formatter must never change meaning
docs.text:
The one rule a formatter cannot break is this: reformatting code must never change what it does. It may move whitespace around, but the program has to mean exactly the same thing afterward.

stenopos fmt broke that rule on multi-line strings. A string can span several lines:

str report = "
    Name: {name}
    Score: {score}
"

The formatter worked one line at a time and re-indented each line to its brace depth. But the indented lines here are inside a string — that leading whitespace is part of the text. Re-indenting them silently rewrote the string's contents.

The fix teaches the formatter to track when it is inside a string that continues onto the next line — the same way it already tracks multi-line block comments. A line that begins inside a string is now left exactly as written, while the code around it still gets tidied. stenopos fmt is idempotent again, and safe on every example we have.

docs.title: Why this happened — and why that's the point
docs.text:
We didn't find this by staring at the formatter. We found it by using it: turning stenopos fmt --check and stenopos lint loose on the whole examples repository and the standard library. One file — a demo of multi-line string interpolation — was exactly the shape that tripped the bug.

That is the whole argument for a language shipping its own tools and then using them on itself. The examples and the standard library are the code new users read first; keeping them consistently formatted and lint-clean matters. And the act of enforcing that is what pulls bugs like this into the light.

docs.title: Staying solid from here
docs.text: Both the examples and the standard library now run a style check on every push: stenopos fmt --check on every file, and stenopos lint on every file that parses. If a contribution drifts out of format or picks up a lint, CI says so before it lands.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

Every release is checksummed and signed. If you're already on beta.6, this is a drop-in upgrade — the only change is a stenopos fmt that no longer touches the inside of your multi-line strings.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.8: FFI, unsafe — and the Language Is Frozen
docs.text: This is a milestone release. beta.8 adds the last two things the language was missing — calling C, and touching raw memory — and with them the v1 feature set is complete. From here, the Rust compiler is frozen: bug fixes only, no new language features, until it is replaced entirely by Stenopos.

docs.title: The escape hatch: FFI and raw pointers
docs.text:
A memory-safe language still has to talk to the world, and the world is written in C. beta.8 adds extern "C" for calling C functions, and raw pointers — ptr[T], address-of &x, dereference *p, and store-through *p = v.

The key design choice is that these live behind a wall. Taking an address is fine, but dereferencing a raw pointer, writing through one, or calling a C function is only allowed inside an unsafe { } block:

extern "C" {
    func abs(int32 n) -> int32
}

func main() -> void {
    int32 x = 41
    unsafe {
        ptr[int32] p = &x
        *p = *p + 1            // read and write through the pointer
    }
    println("x is now: {x}")   // 42

    unsafe {
        println("abs(-7) = {abs(0 - 7)}")
    }
}

Everything outside unsafe still carries the full guarantee. The unsafe blocks are exactly where a reviewer looks first — the boundary is explicit, small, and searchable.

docs.title: The bigger news: the language is feature-complete
docs.text:
FFI + unsafe was the last feature on the list. Take stock of what Stenopos is today: memory safety without a garbage collector, null safety, checked integer overflow, taint tracking, effect and capability typing, constant-time and crypto-sensitivity checks, contracts, structured concurrency with static deadlock-order checking, generics and traits, modules with real visibility, and a built-in formatter, linter, doc generator, and test runner — all in one signed binary. And now C interop and a raw-memory escape hatch.

That is the v1 language. We are done adding to it.

docs.title: What "frozen" means, and what happens next
docs.text:
Stenopos has been able to compile itself for a while — the self-hosting bootstrap holds a byte-for-byte fixpoint. What it couldn't do was compile every other program, because the self-hosted compiler only implements a subset of the language while the Rust compiler kept growing.

Freezing the language stops that chase. Now the self-hosted Stenopos compiler can catch up to a fixed target, feature by feature, until it can compile everything the Rust one can. When it can, the Rust compiler gets deleted — and the first release candidate ships with zero Rust in it. Stenopos, built entirely by Stenopos.

That is the whole point of the project, and today is the day the finish line stopped moving. The checklist from here is public and bounded. See you at rc.1.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

Signed and checksummed, as always.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.9: The Self-Hosted Compiler Caught Up
docs.text:
Two releases ago we froze the language and said the finish line had stopped moving: the Rust compiler would sit still while the Stenopos-written compiler caught up to it, feature by feature, until it could build every program the Rust one could. beta.9 is the release where it caught up.

The self-hosted compiler now compiles and runs the entire example corpus — every single program, none skipped. Everything the reference compiler can build, the compiler written in Stenopos can build too.

docs.title: What "caught up" actually means
docs.text:
Stenopos has been able to compile itself for a long time. That sounds like the whole game, but it isn't — the compiler's own source only uses part of the language, so passing that test just proves the compiler can build one particular program. The real question is whether it can build everything else.

So we kept a bag of test programs — small ones that each lean on a different corner of the language: strings, maps, slices, generics, traits, concurrency, error handling, unsafe code, and so on. The rule is simple and unforgiving: the Stenopos-built compiler has to compile each one, run it, and produce exactly the output the reference compiler does, down to the exit code.

At the start of this stretch it passed 48 of 65. Today it passes all 65, with the self-hosting fixpoint still holding byte-for-byte. The gap is closed.

docs.title: Closing the gap
docs.text:
Most of the remaining programs failed on the same missing piece, so the work was less "seventeen bugs" and more "a handful of real features." The big ones:

  • Real 64-bit integers. This was the deep one. The compiler had been quietly pretending int64 was just a 32-bit int, which works right up until you write a number that doesn't fit — like a five-billion-item count, or a hash seed. int64 is now a true 64-bit type everywhere: in variables, in arithmetic, in lists, maps, arrays, and slices. Teaching the compiler this without breaking its ability to build itself — which uses int64 in hundreds of places — was the trickiest change in the project so far.

  • Unsigned 32-bit integers and overflow that bites. uint32 arrived, along with the guarantee it exists to protect: a plain int32 multiply that overflows now stops the program instead of silently wrapping to a wrong, often-exploitable value. If you actually want wrapping — for a hash or a checksum — you ask for it by name.

  • Slices. A borrowed T[] window into an array: nums[1..<4] hands you a view over three elements without copying anything. Length-checked, iterable, and cheap to pass around.

  • Cleanup that keeps its promises. defer now works with println, and a finally block runs even when a return leaves early — and if there's no catch to handle an error, the finally still runs and the error keeps travelling outward instead of vanishing.

Each of these went in with the whole corpus and the self-hosting fixpoint re-checked at every step, so nothing that already worked quietly broke along the way.

docs.title: What's left
docs.text:
The language is frozen. The self-hosted compiler can now build everything the Rust compiler can. That leaves exactly one thing between here and the first release candidate: making the Stenopos-built compiler the one we actually ship, and then deleting the Rust one. rc.1 is Stenopos, built entirely by Stenopos, with zero Rust inside — and for the first time, that's a packaging job, not a language one.

The finish line isn't just standing still anymore. We're walking up to it.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

Signed and checksummed, as always.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.10: Build Once, Run Anywhere
docs.text: Most of the time you build a program on the same kind of machine you run it on — write it on your laptop, run it on your laptop. But sometimes the machine you are building for is not the one in front of you: a Raspberry Pi, a router, an old server, a phone. beta.10 makes that a single command.

docs.title: One command, eleven CPUs
docs.text:
stenopos build --target aarch64 -o app main.sten

That builds a program for a 64-bit ARM chip — from an ordinary x86 laptop. No extra steps, no fiddling with toolchains by hand.

It works because the compiler doesn't hard-wire a particular CPU into your program until the very last moment. Think of it like a writer who drafts an idea in plain terms first, then hands it to a translator to put into whatever language the reader needs. --target just names the language.

Eleven of them ship in this release:

x86_64, aarch64 (64-bit ARM), ppc64le, riscv64, armv7 (32-bit ARM), s390x, i686 (32-bit x86), powerpc (32-bit), mips, mipsel, and mips64el.

That list covers every combination that matters: 32-bit and 64-bit, and both byte orders (the two ways a CPU can lay out numbers in memory — "little-endian" and the older "big-endian"). Each one is checked the honest way — we cross-build a real program and run it on an emulator of that chip, on every change, so a target on this list will not quietly stop working.

docs.title: A profile for writing, a profile for shipping
docs.text:
A build you're still working on and a build you're ready to hand out want different things. So stenopos build now has two modes.

Plain stenopos build is the draft: fast, and it keeps all the labels on — the function names and debug markers a debugger needs when something goes wrong. It's the manuscript with notes in the margins.

stenopos build --release is the finished book: optimized, and stripped of everything a stranger doesn't need. It also removes the small tells that would reveal the program was written in Stenopos — the internal names and messages are compiled out — so a release binary looks like any other C program. (To be clear: this hides information; the safety and security protections are on in every build, always.)

You can set the default and tweak the details in a stenopos.toml file, so your team just types stenopos build and gets the right thing:

[build]
profile = "draft"

[profile.release]
opt-level = "2"
strip = true

docs.title: A bug we're glad we caught
docs.text:
Getting those eleven CPUs right turned up a real one. On a 32-bit, big-endian chip, a program would crash the moment it allocated memory.

The cause is a nice illustration of why "the same code" isn't the same on every machine. When the program asked the system for a chunk of memory, it passed along the size as a 64-bit number. But on a 32-bit chip, the size is only expected to be 32 bits — half as wide. On a big-endian machine, the half the system actually read was the wrong half: zero. So the program asked for a zero-sized box and then tried to put things in it. Boom.

The fix was to always hand the size across through a small helper that knows the right width for the machine it's on. With that in place, all eleven targets run correctly.

docs.title: Also new
docs.text:
• stenopos dump-tokens and stenopos dump-ast show you exactly how the compiler reads your file — the first tools you reach for when a program parses in a way you didn't expect.
  • stenopos build --verify-ir runs a quick self-check on the compiler's internal work before it produces a binary, catching malformed output early.
  • A new fuzzer runs on every change, generating random programs and checking that the two compilers (the original and the self-hosted one) agree on every one.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

Binaries for all six shipped architectures are attached to the GitHub release, each checksummed and signed. And once it's installed, that one binary can cross-compile your programs to any of the eleven — see Cross-compilation.

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.11: The Compiler Catches More of Your Mistakes
docs.text: The whole promise of Stenopos is that the compiler catches your mistakes before your users do. beta.11 makes it catch a few more — the shipped compiler now rejects the same bad programs the reference compiler always has, and explains them the same way.

docs.title: A little background
docs.text:
Stenopos is written in Stenopos. There are really two compilers: the original one (written in Rust, the "reference"), and the self-hosted one (written in Stenopos, which is what you download). For a long time the self-hosted compiler could build everything the reference could — but it was quietly a bit more lenient: a handful of clearly-wrong programs slipped through it that the reference would have stopped.

For a language whose pitch is "the compiler is on your side," being less strict than the reference is exactly the wrong direction. beta.11 closes the gap.

docs.title: What it now catches
docs.text:
Four kinds of mistake that used to slip through the shipped compiler now stop it:

Returning the wrong type. A function that promises to return an int32 but hands back a true:

func f() -> int32 {
    return true      // error: return type mismatch
}

A match that forgets a case. If you match on an enum, you have to handle every variant (or add a case _). Miss one, and the compiler says so — instead of silently letting a value fall through with nowhere to go:

match (color) {
    case Color.Red: paint_red()
    // error: match is not exhaustive — Green and Blue aren't handled
}

A contract that isn't a yes/no question. @requires and @ensures are boolean conditions; anything else is now rejected:

@requires(n)         // error: a `@requires` contract must be a `bool` expression
func f(int32 n) -> int32 { return n }

A struct built with a field missing. Leave one out and the compiler names it, instead of a confusing punctuation error:

Point p = Point { x: 1 }   // error: struct literal for `Point` is missing field `y`

docs.title: Clearer wording, too
docs.text: A few messages were reworded to match the reference exactly — an unknown name now reads undefined variable `x`, and a type that needs a cast[T]() says "no implicit conversions." Small, but it means every tool and tutorial describes the same error the same way.

docs.title: The proof
docs.text: There's a public suite of example programs — real code and deliberately-broken code — that every release is checked against. As of beta.11 the shipped, self-hosted compiler passes all 55 of them, the broken ones included. What the reference rejects, the compiler you download now rejects too.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

Nothing in your working code needs to change — if your programs were correct, they still compile. beta.11 only turns a few incorrect programs from "compiles anyway" into "here's what's wrong."

docs.title: Stenopos v1.0.0-beta.12: Safer, and Faster
docs.text: Two things a systems language owes you: it shouldn't let you write a memory bug, and it shouldn't make you pay for that safety in speed. beta.12 pushes on both — the compiler catches two more kinds of mistake before your program ever runs, and the code it produces got noticeably faster.

docs.title: Using something before it exists
docs.text:
You can declare a variable and fill it in later. But what if one path forgets to?

func pick() -> int32 {
    int32 x
    if (lucky()) {
        x = 10
    }
    return x        // error: `x` may be used before it is assigned
}

Before, a program like this could read whatever happened to be sitting in memory — the classic source of "works on my machine, crashes on yours," and worse. Now the compiler traces every path through your function, and if even one of them reaches a read without a write first, it stops you and points at the spot. If you meant for it to start at zero, say so (int32 x = 0) — but now that's your choice, not an accident.

(Anything that lives on the heap and is declared without a value is zeroed, so an early read can never hand back a dangling pointer. Safe by construction.)

docs.title: Dividing by zero the compiler can already see
docs.text:
If the compiler can tell the divisor is zero, there's no reason to wait until the program runs to find out:

int32 bad  = 10 / 0        // error: division by zero
int32 also = x % (3 - 3)   // error: division by zero

Divisors it can't know until runtime still trap safely — this just moves the obvious cases to compile time, where a mistake is cheap to fix.

docs.title: Faster, without giving up the checks
docs.text:
Stenopos checks things C doesn't: every array index is in bounds, every +, -, and * is watched for overflow. Those checks are why a whole category of exploits simply can't happen here. The catch has always been that checks cost time.

beta.12 gets most of that time back. For a lot of everyday code, the compiler now proves that a check can never fire — and when it can prove it, it removes the check. A loop that sums an array, a counter that can't overflow, an index that's plainly in range: the safety is still guaranteed, but the machine code comes out the same as the unchecked C you'd have written by hand. Several of our benchmarks that used to run meaningfully slower than C now match it exactly.

You don't switch any of this on. Build your program, and it's just faster.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

As always, correct programs keep working unchanged. beta.12 only turns a few incorrect ones from "compiles, then misbehaves" into "here's the line" — and makes the correct ones run faster on the way out.

docs.title: Stenopos compiles itself, and the Rust is gone
docs.text: v1.0.0-rc.1 is out, and it crosses a line the whole project was pointed at from the start: Stenopos is now written in Stenopos, and nothing else. The compiler that turns your .sten files into programs was itself built by a compiler written in the same language — no Rust anywhere.

docs.title: How a language gets off the ground
docs.text:
Every new language faces the same chicken-and-egg problem. To compile Stenopos, you need a Stenopos compiler. But to write the compiler in Stenopos, you'd need a Stenopos compiler to compile it. Something has to come first.

So Stenopos started with a seed: a compiler for Stenopos, written in Rust. It wasn't the goal — it was scaffolding. Its only job was to compile the real compiler, the one written in Stenopos, until that one could stand on its own.

For the last stretch of betas, that's exactly what happened. The Stenopos-written compiler learned to build everything the Rust seed could, then to reject the same mistakes the same way, and lately to run some things faster than the seed did. It quietly became the compiler you actually download.

docs.title: What just changed
docs.text:
With rc.1, the scaffolding comes down. The Rust seed — about 66,000 lines — is deleted. What's left builds itself:

  • The compiler compiles its own source into a new compiler.
  • That new compiler compiles the source again.
  • The two outputs come out byte-for-byte identical — a fixed point. That's the proof it's stable: a compiler that reproduces itself exactly.

Think of it like a printing press that can print the complete plans for building another press just like it — and the copy it prints is indistinguishable from the original. Once you have one working press, you never need the workshop that built the first one again.

To make that reproducible for anyone, each release ships a seed of record: one trusted, prebuilt Stenopos binary. Point the build at it and it reconstructs the whole compiler from source, start to finish, with no Rust toolchain on the machine at all. We even run the build with cargo and rustc replaced by tripwires that fail if anything tries to call them — and it sails through.

docs.title: What this means for you
docs.text:
Nothing in your code has to change. The language is the same, your programs compile and run the same, and the binaries you download work the same way. This is a change in how the compiler is made, not in what it does.

What it buys the project is honesty and independence: the tool that promises to catch your mistakes is now held to its own promises. Every safety guarantee Stenopos makes — memory safety, checked arithmetic, taint tracking — the compiler's own source code lives under. It eats its own cooking.

docs.title: The road here, briefly
docs.text: The betas were the climb: null safety, the trait system, diagnostics that match to the letter, six shipped CPU architectures, checked-overflow and bounds elision that claw back the speed, and last-use move elision. Every one of those had to work in the Stenopos-written compiler before the Rust could go. rc.1 is where the ladder gets kicked away.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

A release candidate means we think this is what 1.0 looks like. If your programs were correct, they still are — now built by a compiler that speaks its own language.

docs.title: rc.2: closures, a security type system, and a smarter scheduler
docs.text:
v1.0.0-rc.2 is the biggest feature release since the language started compiling itself. Three things landed at once — lambdas, a security type system you can actually feel at compile time, and a concurrency scheduler that stops treating every background task as a brand-new operating-system thread.

Everything here was written in Stenopos, compiled by Stenopos, and checked the same way every release is: the compiler builds itself twice and the two results come out byte-for-byte identical.

docs.title: Lambdas: functions you can hand around
docs.text:
Until now, a function was a thing you named and called. You couldn't pick one up and pass it somewhere. Now you can:

List[int32] xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
List[int32] doubled = xs.map(|x| -> int32 x * 2)   // 2 4 6 8 10
List[int32] evens   = xs.filter(|x| x % 2 == 0)     // 2 4
int32 total         = xs.reduce(0, |acc, x| acc + x) // 15

A |x| ... is a lambda — a small function written right where you use it. It can also capture values from around it (by copy, so the original is never disturbed):

int32 factor = 10
fn(int32)->int32 scale = |x| -> int32 x * factor   // remembers factor = 10

map, filter, and reduce on lists come along for free. The type fn(int32)->int32 is a real type you can store in a variable, pass to a function, or return from one.

docs.title: A type system that enforces security
docs.text:
This is the part we're most excited about. Stenopos now tracks, at compile time, five different ways code can go wrong with sensitive data — and refuses to build a program that gets them wrong.

  • @sensitive wipes secrets. Mark a value @sensitive and its memory is zeroed the moment it's done being used, so a key or password can't linger in freed memory for a crash dump or a later read to find.

  • Capability tokens (cap[R]). A function can only touch the filesystem, the network, and so on if it is handed a token for it. You can't conjure one out of thin air — only trusted code mints them, and they're passed along explicitly. Code that was never given the token simply cannot reach the resource.

  • An effect lattice (@pure → @io → @net). Label a function with what it's allowed to do and the compiler checks it — and everything it calls — stays inside that box. A @pure function provably does nothing you can observe; an @io function provably never opens a socket.

  • Constant-time secrets (secret[T]). A secret[int32] can't be used in a way whose timing would leak it — no branching on it, no using it as an array index, no division. You get ct_select to choose between two values without a branch, and declassify to say, out loud and on the record, "I am revealing this now."

  • --obfuscate. Build with this flag and the text strings in your program are scrambled on disk, so running strings on the binary turns up nothing. They're unscrambled in memory the instant the program starts.

None of this slows down code that doesn't opt in. It's there when you reach for it.

docs.title: Hemerodromes that reuse threads
docs.text:
spawn starts a Hemerodrome — a concurrent unit of work. Before rc.2, every spawn created a fresh operating-system thread. That's fine for a handful; it's wasteful for thousands.

Now Hemerodromes run on a pool of worker threads that get reused. When you spawn work, an idle worker picks it up; the pool only grows a new thread when every worker is already busy. So short tasks stop costing a whole thread each, and a task that blocks can never starve the others — the behavior is never worse than before, and usually much better. Your code doesn't change at all; spawn, channels, and locks work exactly as they did.

Along the way we found and fixed a quiet bug: the machinery behind try/catch was shared across threads when it shouldn't have been. Each Hemerodrome now has its own, so a throw in one can never trip over another's. The thread-safety checkers agree it's clean.

docs.title: Getting it
docs.text:
Same as always — grab the compiler, point it at a .sten file, and run it. The full list of changes is in the release notes.

Next up: inline assembly, which unlocks the last piece of the scheduler and a path to running Stenopos with no C runtime underneath at all.

docs.title: rc.3: a language server, data that moves between threads, and raw assembly
docs.text:
v1.0.0-rc.3 makes Stenopos feel like a language you live in, not just one you compile with. Your editor now understands it, concurrent tasks can hand real data back and forth without copying or races, and — for the rare moments you need it — you can drop all the way down to raw machine instructions.

As always, everything here was written in Stenopos, compiled by Stenopos, and checked the same way: the compiler builds itself twice and the two results come out byte-for-byte identical.

docs.title: Your editor now understands Stenopos
docs.text:
Stenopos ships a language server. Point any editor that speaks LSP — VS Code, Neovim, and most others — at stenopos lsp, and you get:

  • Live error checking. As you type, mistakes get a red underline with the real compiler's message — the exact same check that runs at build time, not a rough imitation. Fix the problem and the underline disappears.
  • Hover a name to see what it is.
  • Jump to definition of a function, struct, or enum.
  • Completion for keywords, built-ins, and the names in your file.

It's one command — the language server is built into the stenopos binary, nothing extra to install. Setup for Neovim and VS Code is in the tooling reference.

docs.title: Passing real data between Hemerodromes
docs.text:
A Hemerodrome is a concurrent unit of work you start with spawn. Until now, the mailbox between Hemerodromes — a channel — could only carry simple numbers. Now it carries real things: text, structs, lists, and maps.

chan[str] ch = chan()
spawn producer(ch)
str msg = ch.recv()        // a whole string arrives, safely

The trick is a simple rule: sending gives the value away. When you send something down a channel, the sender no longer owns it — the receiver does. There is never a moment where two Hemerodromes both hold the same piece of memory, so there's no race and nothing gets freed twice. The compiler enforces this for you; if you want to keep a copy, you say so with .clone(). And because sending is a handover, not a copy, it costs the same whether you send three characters or three megabytes.

Locks learned the same lesson. A mutex[Point] can guard a real struct, and you can change it in place while you hold the lock — no copying it out and back:

with (p = m.borrow()) {
    p.x = p.x + 1          // changed right where it lives, under the lock
}

That borrow is fenced in: the compiler won't let the pointer escape the locked section, so you can't accidentally keep using it after the lock is released. There's a read-only version, read_borrow(), for when many readers just want to look.

docs.title: Inline assembly
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to say exactly what the machine does. asm { } lets you write raw instructions, with the GCC-style operand syntax for feeding values in and getting them out:

unsafe {
    asm {
        "addl %1, %0"
        : "=r"(sum)
        : "r"(a), "r"(b)
    }
}

It's gated behind unsafe, because it is. This is the last piece the green-thread scheduler needed for its hand-written context switch — and it opens the path to running Stenopos with no C runtime underneath at all.

docs.title: Smaller and quicker, too
docs.text: Calls between functions in the same program now go directly to their target instead of through an indirection table, the way a C compiler does it — a little less overhead and a little smaller on disk, for free.

docs.title: Getting it
docs.text:
Same as always — grab the compiler, point it at a .sten file, and run it. The full list of changes is in the release notes.

Next up: making the editor smarts deeper — hover and go-to-definition that follow the compiler's full understanding of your code, across files — and the final polish on the road to 1.0.

docs.title: rc.4: a smarter editor, and three silent mistakes turned into errors
docs.text: v1.0.0-rc.4 is a stabilization release. The language server now understands your code the way the compiler does, across files, and three cases where the compiler quietly produced the wrong program now stop with a clear error.

docs.title: The editor follows your imports
docs.text:
Hover, go to definition and completion are now built on the compiler's own lexer rather than a text search. They find functions, methods, structs, classes, enums and traits, including signatures that span several lines; they ignore func inside a comment or a string; and they keep working while the file is half-typed and doesn't compile yet.

They also reach across files: go to definition on an imported name jumps into the module that defines it, hover shows its signature from there, and completion offers the module's public names.

docs.title: No more silent mis-compiles
docs.text:
• An unknown type is an error. Widget w = … with Widget undefined or misspelled used to fall back to int32 and read garbage. It now says "unknown type Widget".
  • auto is an error. Type inference isn't implemented yet, and auto x = 42 used to compile into a garbage-typed variable. It now asks you to write the type.
  • spawn with one argument works. spawn worker(42) silently never ran; it does now.

docs.title: rc.5: tagma, editions and one download for everything
docs.text: v1.0.0-rc.5 gives Stenopos a build tool. Syntagma now ships two commands: tagma, which you use day to day for projects, and stenopos, the compiler, for single files.

docs.title: Projects with tagma
docs.text:
tagma new hello
cd hello
tagma run          # Hello from hello!

A project is a directory with a Tagma.toml:

[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2026"

[dependencies]
util = { path = "../util" }

tagma build, run, check, test, fmt, lint, doc and clean all work on the whole project. Dependencies are local paths for now; the package registry arrives in rc.6. See Projects with tagma.

docs.title: Editions
docs.text: The language now changes through editions. A project names the one it is written in, and 2026 is the first. One compiler accepts every edition it knows, and breaking changes only ever come with a new edition that you opt into.

docs.title: One download
docs.text:
Each release now ships a bundle per architecture, syntagma-<version>-linux-<arch>.tar.gz, with tagma, stenopos, the runtime and a pinned standard library. The installer installs it, and both commands find their runtime and library beside themselves, wherever you put them.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Stenopos/Syntagma/main/install.sh | sh

docs.title: Also
docs.text:
• The compiler's source moved from selfhost/ to compiler/.
  • The easter eggs moved to tagma. Try tagma sparta.

docs.title: rc.6: packages you can trust with exactly what you grant
docs.text: v1.0.0-rc.6 brings the package registry. A project can depend on published packages, and each one gets only the capabilities you grant it, enforced by the compiler on its code.

docs.title: Using packages
docs.text:
The first package, stenopos/dotenv, is written and tested, and will be published to the registry shortly after this release. Adding it will look like this:

$ tagma add stenopos/dotenv
       Added dotenv = stenopos/dotenv 1.0.0 (granted File)

tagma add writes one line to Tagma.toml and grants the package what it and its dependencies use:

[dependencies]
dotenv = { package = "stenopos/dotenv", version = "1.0.0", allow = ["File"] }

Take File away and the build stops, naming the package and the capability. A dependency can only pass on to its own dependencies what it was granted, and the compiler holds every package's source to its limit: unsafe needs Memory, extern and asm need System.

tagma update moves to the newest version of each major version, tagma remove drops a dependency, and tagma vendor copies everything into vendor/ for builds with no network. Versions are chosen by minimal version selection and recorded in Tagma.lock with each package's commit and content hash; every build checks the files against it.

See Packages and the registry.

docs.title: A registry with no server
docs.text:
The registry is a signed git index that records where each version's source lives and a hash of its files:

  • The root key, kept offline, approves the keys that sign; a snapshot signed daily expires after seven days, so a frozen or replayed index is refused.
  • Each version is published by CI from a signed tag: CI tests it, finds the capabilities its code uses (tagma caps), signs the entry, and the registry's own CI re-derives the entry from the source before accepting it.
  • A broken version can be retracted; a compromised publisher key can be revoked, which revokes what it signed from then on, even from existing lock files.

docs.title: Also in rc.6
docs.text:
• Language: function types over any type (fn(List[int32]) -> int32), named functions as values, ordering for str, a lazy and chainable ??, struct parameters that borrow, and str_from_byte (std builds UTF-8 and any bytes on it).
  • Memory: every example, course program and test suite now runs under valgrind in CI, and so does the toolchain itself. Leaks found that way are fixed: discard, clear(), pop() of a struct, and temporaries passed to calls.
  • std: std.toml reads every TOML escape, rejects what TOML forbids, and is fuzzed against Python's tomllib on every build.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Every release from now on shows how it compares with C, measured by CI on the tagged commit. Since rc.5:

  • Strings are built in one allocation. A chain of + or an interpolation sums its parts' lengths and copies each part once, where each + used to copy the whole string so far; integers are formatted without snprintf. The string-heavy benchmarks (strings, map, structs) run 44–56% fewer instructions.
  • Overflow checks cost less. Checked arithmetic no longer makes every call of a function save registers it only needs on some paths: recursive fib runs 20% fewer instructions.
  • Smaller binaries. Release builds drop the code a program never calls, such as the copy and drop helpers for struct types it doesn't copy.
  • Faster builds. The compiler's own work on a small build is down by up to 41%: it no longer starts extra processes to check which LLVM it is using, and release builds pass LLVM bitcode instead of text.
  • Loops don't grow the stack. A loop that built strings used a new stack slot on every iteration; a long one could overflow a task's stack.

Each program is written twice, in Stenopos and in C, and both must print the same output. Stenopos builds with stenopos build --release, C with cc -O2 -s. docs.title: rc.7: programs that run as services
docs.text: v1.0.0-rc.7 is about programs that run until they are told to stop: an HTTP endpoint, a worker, a connection to a device, and a clean exit when Kubernetes sends SIGTERM. Everything a service needs is in the standard library now, written in Stenopos, and none of it needs a shell.

docs.title: Tasks that wait
docs.text:
A Hemerodrome (a spawned task) that sleeps, or waits on a socket, a channel, a child process or a signal, now parks: its worker thread runs the other tasks meanwhile. A server, a timer and a client run together on a single thread. Every wait can have a deadline:

str? job = jobs.recv_timeout(10000)     // null: nothing within 10 s
str? got = recv_timeout(conn, 5000)     // the same for a socket

Functions can return a channel they created (start a worker, hand back its channel), and spawn takes str arguments.

docs.title: HTTP and TLS
docs.text:
std.http is a server and a client. The server runs one task per connection with keep-alive, size limits and a timeout per read; the client (std.http.client) speaks http and https and decodes chunked bodies. Both read framing strictly (RFC 9112): anything two parsers could read differently, which is how requests are smuggled, is refused. CI fuzzes them against Python's parsers and attacks a live server on every build.

std.tls uses the system's OpenSSL, linked only into programs that use TLS, and speaks TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. Trust a server through the CAs (verified()), or pin a device's self-signed certificate (pinned("5f:3a:...")), checked before anything is sent. Checking nothing is refused.

docs.title: Stopping cleanly
docs.text:
chan[int32] stop = chan()
notify_signals([SIGTERM, SIGINT], stop)
// ... when stop has a signal: finish the work in hand, then
exit(0)

Returning from main waits for every task, so work a program started is always finished. A program still waiting 3 s after main returned says so; exit_grace(ms) sets a limit. exit() frees what the program holds before it ends: worker threads, OpenSSL's tables, the runtime's own buffers.

See Writing a service.

docs.title: Security fixes
docs.text:
A review of the whole project on 2026-11-14 found four critical problems, all fixed in this release. Two of them are in rc.6: don't run rc.6's tagma check, tagma build or stenopos check on a project you don't trust.

  • Commands from names in a project tree. tagma and stenopos check built shell command lines from paths and package names, so $(...) in a directory or dependency name ran. Every value is now quoted, package names are checked, and the bootstrap builds a hostile tree on every run. rc.8 removes the shell from the toolchain entirely.
  • A use-after-free through !!. !! on a nullable struct handed out the nullable's own storage; it now gives a copy.
  • A server killed from outside. An uncaught error in any task aborted the process, and accept threw when descriptors ran out, so a few hundred idle connections stopped any std.http service. An uncaught error now ends the program cleanly (exit 70, documented), and accept rides out descriptor exhaustion.
  • Request and response splitting. std.http sends no CR, LF or NUL from a program's values in a request or response.

One more was found by our own fuzzing while the release was being built: std.http trimmed control bytes away before reading a header or a chunk size, so Content-Length: 1 followed by a control byte read as 1, where other HTTP parsers refuse it. Two parsers that disagree about where a message ends is how requests are smuggled past a proxy. A start line or header with any control byte but tab is now refused, and chunk sizes are read strictly.

Also from the review: TLS setup steps fail closed and a closed connection's handle can't reach a newer one; every allocation in the runtime is checked (stenopos: out of memory instead of a crash later); exit() no longer cleans up OpenSSL under a task still using it; and output is flushed line by line when it goes to a pipe, so kubectl logs shows each line as it is printed.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Every program used to start twice: it raised its stack limit to 1 GiB and executed itself again, which made a hello-world take 1.7 times as long as C's (3.1 ms against 1.8 ms). Programs now run on the system's stack, as C programs do; one that needs more says so ([build] stack = "256MiB" in Tagma.toml), and a stack overflow says so instead of a bare segmentation fault.

Every allocation is now checked, and allocating got cheaper anyway: the check costs one test, the runtime calls libc without PLT stubs, and integers become strings without a copy. Measured by CI against rc.6, the map benchmark runs 2.0% fewer instructions and strings 2.5%.

One number went the wrong way: the map binary grew from 14 KB to 18 KB. Binaries grow a page (4 KB) at a time, and this release's runtime additions put map's code just past a page boundary, by about 340 bytes. rc.8 brings it back under, as the first step of the size work in the plan. The compiler's own work grew 1.1%.

Each program is written twice, in Stenopos and in C, and both must print the same output. Stenopos builds with stenopos build --release, C with cc -O2 -s. docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
What this release does not do yet, each with its plan:

  • A function that creates a channel, lock or atomic and doesn't return it waits for every task in the program when it returns. In a service, create them in main. rc.8 makes them reference counted.
  • Using a value after send moved it isn't refused at compile time.
  • std.http's timeout is per read, and connections aren't capped: put a public service behind a proxy.
  • Taint tracking covers the functions you mark; the standard library's sources and sinks are marked by 1.0.

docs.title: Files, programs and time
docs.text: std.fs (read, write_atomic, append, list_dir, stat, ...), std.os.execute(["tar", "-czf", out, dir]) (no shell: an argument is never interpreted), std.time (clocks, sleeping, UTC and local formatting), and std.net by name, IPv4 or IPv6, with failures that say why: connect mosquitto:1883: connection refused.

docs.title: tagma
docs.text:
• Progress lines go to stderr, so tagma run > out.txt holds only the program's output. [output] in Tagma.toml sends them to stdout or nowhere, and log = "logs/build.log" keeps a log of every run, the compiler's diagnostics included.
  • tagma doc --prepare gives every file, type and function a /// doc block (existing comments become docs; the rest get stubs), and tagma doc --check fails while a public item is undocumented. Every public item in the standard library is documented.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A program's functions were taken as part of the last module it imported (duplicate function 'rfc3339' in module 'std.time').
  • A module imported both directly and by another import could be placed after its user ("unknown type Conn").
  • read_file read /proc and /sys files as empty.
  • std.logging's file logger and std.io.append_file rewrote the whole file for every line; they append in one write now.
  • Escapes: \xNN and \u{...} exist, and an unknown escape is an error.

The full list is in the CHANGELOG.
